articles.title: Polanski heckled at Jewish community hustings after saying that Zionism is a form of racism – UK politics live
articles.summary:
The Green leader, who is Jewish, made the remarks as part of his campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection

Morning, and welcome to our UK politics live blog.

Zack…

image.caption: Leader of the Green party of England and Wales, Zack Polanski Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA

blocks.text: Polanski heckled as he declares himself an anti-Zionist at byelection hustings
Morning, and welcome to our UK politics live blog.

Zack Polanski declared himself an anti-Zionist and faced heckling at a Jewish community hustings in Holborn and St Pancras, where the Green party leader is standing as a candidate in next month’s byelection.

He said Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – was a form of racism because it involved the displacement and genocide of Palestinians. His remarks were met with boos from the audience last night.

blocks.caption: Zack Polanski said he was an anti-Zionist during a by-election hustings event at a Jewish community centre in Holborn and St Pancras. Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/Alamy

blocks.text: “I’m an anti-Zionist. I think countries have always been ideas and I think things change over time,” he said.

Polanski, who is Jewish, said criticising the Israeli government and the occupation of Palestinian land was not antisemitic. “We need to come together to recognise that when we call that antisemitic, we are making ourselves as Jewish people less safe,” he added.

As the Green party prepares for its annual conference, members are due to vote on a motion to declare Zionism as a form of racism in official policy. As my colleague Peter Walker reported last week, some in the party fear it could alienate Jewish supporters if it passed:

double quotation markA Green official said that many activists loyal to the party’s leadership might not be at the autumn conference because it takes place a week before voting in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, in which Polanski hopes to take Keir Starmer’s old seat from Labour, potentially leaving more scope for others to push through the motion. “The risk is that if it passes as it is we are alienating ourselves from the Jewish community in the UK, a lot of whom are not big fans of the current Israeli government,” a Green source said. There was, they added, a parallel worry about internal splits, with some Green activists in leaked WhatsApp chats warning that Polanski was “struggling to overcome Zionist indoctrination”.

articles.title: SC asked to void lowered vote threshold in Sara Duterte impeachment
articles.summary: Two petitions have been filed before the Supreme Court challenging the lowered voting threshold approved by the Senate impeachment court to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 5:52pm
The main building of the Philippine Supreme Court in Manila.
Philstar.com / Martin Ramos
MANILA, Philippines — Two petitions have been filed before the Supreme Court challenging the lowered voting threshold approved by the Senate impeachment court to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.
Lawyer Ernesto Francisco filed his petition on Friday, September 25, while former Executive Secretary Vic Rodriguez filed his petition on Thursday, September 24.
Both petitioners urged the Supreme Court to intervene immediately rather than wait for the trial's conclusion.
They argued that allowing a potentially unconstitutional voting standard to decide the Vice President's fate could plunge the nation into severe political chaos and instability.
Francisco asked the High Court to declare the September 23 Senate proceedings null and void and issue a Status Quo Ante Order.

Rodriguez similarly prayed for a temporary restraining order to restrain the Senate from conducting or giving effect to any final conviction vote under the reduced denominator, asking the Court to reinstate the July 6 ruling requiring a strict 16-vote threshold.
Both petitioners argue that the Senate has overstepped its constitutional boundaries.
For Francisco, he said that the Senate impeachment court's ruling is a "capricious, arbitrary and whimsical interpretation" that amounts to a constitutional amendment.

"Substituting 'all members of the Senate' with 'those members who... remain legally and factually capable of participating' constitutes a rewriting of the Constitution, which the public respondent Senate Impeachment Court cannot legally do," Francisco said.

He warned that allowing the voting threshold to fluctuate based on individual circumstances threatens the structural integrity of other legislative voting requirements, such as declaring a state of war, overriding presidential vetoes, or passing tax exemptions.
Rodriguez, on his part, argued that the Senate cannot bypass the formal amendment and revision processes mandated under Article XVII of the Constitution.
"The Constitution does not recognize an 'impeachment exception' to its own amendment provisions," Rodriguez said.

The Senate impeachment court on September 22 lowered the voting threshold to convict Duterte, ruling that senators unable to take part in her trial will no longer count toward the two-thirds required by the Constitution.

articles.title: Sandiganbayan orders Romualdez to show up on October 12 bail hearing
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan has ordered former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez to appear before the anti-graft court on October 12 for the first day of his bail hearing.

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 5:51pm
The Sandiganbayan has ordered former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez to appear before the anti-graft court on October 12 for the first day of his bail hearing.

This was contained in the Sandiganbayan Third Division’s order issued Friday, September 25, in connection with the P7.4-billion plunder charge filed against Romualdez and three others over their alleged links to the flood control controversy.

“Accused Romualdez is required to be present and sign the pre-trial order during the initial bail hearing on October 12, 2026, at 8:30 in the morning,” read the court order, which was issued after the termination of the pre-trial conference or the court process where the evidence for both parties are marked, read.

The anti-graft court also said in the same order that Romualdez is expected to file his petition for bail on Monday, September 28, an information that was also told to reporters by Romualdez’s counsel, Ade Fajardo.
Romualdez attended the pre-trial conference virtually from his cell in New Quezon City Jail on Friday since he is still being treated for his brain and heart-related ailments.

Accordingly, the Sandiganbayan set the bail hearings on the Romualdez case on October 12, 2026, and every Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday thereafter, except on legal holidays and on the day the court has an official activity, all at 8:30 in the morning and 1:30 in the afternoon.
The prosecution, for its part, is expected to present 23 witnesses during the bail hearings.
The anti-graft court ordered the prosecution to submit its list of by Friday, October 2, 2026, alongside the schedule indicating which witnesses will be presented on each hearing date.
The presentation of evidence for the P7.4 billion case, on the other hand, is set on November 23, 2026, and every Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday thereafter. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
articles.summary: The EU had said X "deceives users" by selling blue ticks without "meaningfully verifying" accounts.

blocks.text: The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges.

In December 2025, the European Commission said the platform "deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a blue verified check mark, because it is not "meaningfully verifying" who is behind the account.
But US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said on Thursday that the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to expand its reach to American companies outside its control.
Musk, who spent millions helping elect Donald Trump and other Republicans, has previously claimed EU tech regulation "inhibits progress" for companies.
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed an application, external with the EU's General Court in support of Musk's and X's attempts to dismiss ​the case.

It claims that under a section of law in the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU, a state may intervene in disputes before the court if it "can establish an interest in the result of the case to the court".
The DOJ said the US "has a clear interest" in ensuring any decision by the commission was applied consistently with "how territorial jurisdiction is generally understood in international law".
It also wants to make sure it would not "otherwise prejudice" US-headquartered digital services that "contribute significantly" to its economy.
In a press briefing on Friday, external, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said it was "ready to defend" its position in court.
He added that the commission had an "solid case" at its disposal, due to the alleged breach of its Digital Services Act.
In addition to its use of blue ticks, EU regulators had accused X of failing to provide transparency around its adverts and denying researchers access to public data.

Henna Virkkunen, the regulator's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said at the time of the fine's issue it was "holding X responsible for undermining users' rights and evading accountability".
"Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU," she said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had criticised the EU regulator, accusing it of attacking and censoring US firms.
"The European Commission's fine isn't just an attack on X, it's an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments," Rubio wrote in a post on X.
"The days of censoring Americans online are over."
His remarks were reposted by Musk, who added "absolutely".
The European Commission denied targeting any specific nationality, stating it is simply protecting its digital and democratic standards to maintain its role as a global benchmark.
The action marked the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act (DSA), one of two mandatory rulebooks governing online platforms in the EU.

However, the EU is also conducting several other investigations into the platform, including one into its integrated AI assistant Grok over concerns it was used to create sexualised images of real people.

articles.title: Carlos Yulo falls short of parallel bars medal, concludes stellar Asian Games
articles.summary: Carlos Yulo narrowly misses out on a parallel bars bronze that would have been the cherry on top of his superb Asian Games run that saw him win back-to-back gold medals in floor exercise and vault

blocks.text: FOCUSED. The Philippines' Carlos Edriel Yulo in action during the men's parallel bars final of the Asian Games.
Edgar Su/REUTERS
Carlos Yulo narrowly misses out on a parallel bars bronze that would have been the cherry on top of his superb Asian Games run that saw him win back-to-back gold medals in floor exercise and vault
MANILA, Philippines – It may not have been the perfect ending, but Carlos Yulo has already given the country plenty of reasons to celebrate.

Yulo fell short of a third artistic gymnastics medal as he wrapped up his campaign in the 2026 Asian Games with a fourth-place finish in the men’s parallel bars at the Nagoya General Gymnasium on Friday, September 25.

The double Olympic gold medalist registered 14.3 points, just barely missing out on a bronze that would have been the cherry on top of a superb Asian Games run that saw him win back-to-back gold medals in floor exercise and vault.

With hardly any surprise, reigning two-time Olympic champion Zou Jingyuan struck gold with an unrivaled 15.5 points — a full point ahead of Japan’s Shinnosuke, who settled for silver with 14.5 points.
Zou completed an Asian Games three-peat in the apparatus after also reigning in 2018 in Indonesia and in 2023 in China.
Uzbekistan’s Rasuljon Abdurakhimov edged Yulo for the bronze with 14.433 points.
Despite coming up short, Yulo has done his part, breaking the Philippines’ golden ice in this Asian Games with not just one, but two titles in his pet events.

In fact, Yulo is the only athlete in men’s artistic gymnastics to win gold medals in multiple apparatuses in this edition. Zou and Chinese teammates Zhang Boheng and Lan Xingyu also own two golds, although the other came in the team event.

With his latest triumphs, Yulo has completed his collection, adding a pair of Asian Games golds to a trophy case already filled with titles from the Olympics, World Championships, Asian Championships, World Cup, and Southeast Asian Games. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Volkswagen, Audi to recall almost 1 million cars in Germany
articles.summary: Volkswagen and its subsidiary Audi are to recall nearly a million vehicles in Germany due to a potential steering fault.

image.caption: Volkswagen is to recall nearly a million vehicles in Germany due to a potential steering faultImage: Moritz Frankenberg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany auto firm Volkswagen (VW) and its daughter company Audi are to recall nearly a million vehicles in Germany due to steering problems, according to German media reports.

The KBA road traffic authority was cited by the t-online news portal as saying that the recall was required due to potential bolt failures that could damage the steering gearbox or, in some cases, cause a complete loss of steering.
The bolts are to be replaced with ones resistant to corrosion caused by humidity.
Autor Motor Sport magazine reported that VW believed the steering issue would impact only a smaller proportion of the recalled vehicles.
The company said there were no known cases of accidents or injuries caused by the possible bolt failure.
According to KBA, the VW models Tiguan, Touran, Golf Variant, Caddy und Golf produced between September 24, 2013, and July 1, 2024, are impacted by the recall.
This is equivalent to around 900,000 vehicles in Germany and 2.16 million around the world.
For Audi, 700,000 vehicles around the world are impacted by the problem, including 58,555 in Germany.
The recall comes as VW grapples with dwindling sales in recent years, with the firm laying off tens of thousands of staff and shrinking plants in order to cut costs.

articles.title: Why farmers are pairing crops with solar panels
articles.summary: From cooler soil to paid grazing land, farmers are finding solar panels can do more than generate power.

image.caption: An agrivoltaic pilot project shades a pear orchard in Llupia, France, part of a push to protect crops from droughts, frost and other extreme weatherImage: Michel Clementz/MAXPPP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Traditionally, solar panel farms are quiet — save for the faint hum of the inverter. But on about one in ten of American solar farms, there's a new sound reverberating through fields: baaaa.
Letting sheep roam under solar panels is just one of many forms of a burgeoning strategy called agrivoltaics, where crops grow or livestock graze in tandem with renewable energy infrastructure.

It's not only of potential benefit for the animals, which get additional shade. The panels can also protect crops from the elements as well as divert water to them, creating cooler, damper conditions that even boost yields.
And even the solar panels themselves tend to respond well to this co-existence — as the cooler they are, the more electricity they produce per watt of sunlight.

"Having concrete or something underneath the solar panels — you're going to have lower efficiency than having something like plants that are transpiring and cooling off on the land surface," Carl Bernacchi, professor of plant biology and crop sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, told DW.

While the potential is enormous, especially as climate change puts more and more heat stress on agriculture, the practice is still in its infancy. In Europe, if agrivoltaics were implemented on just 1% of available agricultural land, the continent could exceed its solar energy targets for 2030.
But uptake has been slow: agrivoltaics represents just 18.4 gigawatts of energy worldwide as of mid-2025, less than 1% of the world's solar capacity.

blocks.caption: Sheep graze under solar panels in Guizhou province, southwest China, part of a growing practice of pairing livestock with solar energy productionImage: Tao Liang/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: What thrives under the panels

The idea for agrivoltaics dates back to 1981, when two German scientists published an article titled "Kartoffeln unter dem Kollektor" (or "Potatoes beneath the collector"). But the first pilot project didn't begin until 2004 in Japan, a land-constrained country, where there's particular concern over balancing solar deployment with the protection of farmland.

There are three main types of agrivoltaics: horizontal, where panels look directly up at the sky, vertical, where they're placed in large rows, perpendicular to the ground, and integrated, often installed atop greenhouses.
Research suggests shade-tolerant crops stand to benefit. That includes berries, grapes and tomatoes — where the panels' steel framing often doubles as trellises — as well as peaches and peppers.
The panels can also prevent water from fully evaporating, creating a more humid microclimate that benefits the soil — though humidity is a double-edged sword, sometimes introducing plant disease.

Sheep have also proven to be a particularly good match. Compared to cattle or goats, they're generally easier to manage around solar infrastructure, less likely to damage equipment, and small enough to fit comfortably beneath panels. The practice has other sustainability upsides too: sheep manure fertilizes the soil, and sites require less herbicide.

"If we look at the sheep industry, this has been a real paradigm shift for them, where instead of having to pay to lease land to graze their animals — now they're actually getting paid to graze," Kinzer said. "So it completely puts the economics on its head and is a huge opportunity for the sheep industry, which is really struggling in the US pretty much since World War II."

blocks.caption: Solar panels raised on steel supports shade a French orchard, one of several agrivoltaic setups now in use across EuropeImage: Michel Clementz/MAXPPP/picture alliance

blocks.text: A double climate win
Agrivoltaics sit at a rare intersection of climate mitigation (cutting emissions) and adaptation (adjusting to a warming planet).
"It is both, which is pretty unique as far as climate solutions go," Kinzer said.

The practice offers one answer to where solar panels could go, helping to produce cheaper and more efficient energy, while also benefiting crops that might struggle due to rising temperatures or volatile weather.

And research suggests that climate change will only make regions grow drier, "broadening areas where agrivoltaics can mitigate crop yield penalties (even boosting yield) and improve overall profitability," writeresearchers in a journal article for Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).
A dual-income stream can also offer farmers some insurance should temperature or weather knock out a season's plantings.
"Being able to have that alternate form of income, it's massive for folks who are depending on weather to make their living that is becoming increasingly more extreme and varied," Kinzer said.
Tamil Nadu farmers learn to thrive despite water scarcity
Not every farm benefits
So why has adoption been so slow?
"In theory, it's a win-win scenario," Bernacchi said. "But of course, with any technologies, there are always caveats and issues."

One reason is that agrivoltaics don't work everywhere. In America's arid West, where heat stress and less available water can threaten crops, yields stayed the same or even rose under panels. In the humid Midwest, on the other hand, panel shading limited photosynthesis and led to reduced yields in maize and soybeans.
For cash crops, where there's a very small margin for profit, even a minor reduction in yield is a no-go for many farmers.

Then there's the expense. For solar producers, every added inch to mount panels higher means more labor and steel costs. And farmers might need to find new equipment or change methods to adapt to a new system.

"Farmers want to learn from other farmers," said Kinzer, who works with farmers across the US to see how agrivoltaics are being adopted. "They want to hear from folks who are doing it. And so there's a little bit of a chicken-and-the-egg problem for farmers: In most cases, they can't just go across the street or into the next county over and see a project like this and talk to the farmers doing it."
Bridging the divide between farmers and solar

Solar power's land footprint has made it controversial in certain communities — some farming associations have protested converting farmland into acres of solar panels, arguing their members cease to be farmers and become energy producers instead.
It's a tension agrivoltaics helps to address.

One surveyfound that more than 80% of Americans would be more likely to support solar development in their community, if it allowed for the co-production of energy and agriculture — about 10% more than those that support solar development in general.

"There's this cultural conflict between the farmers who want to farm and the solar companies that want to produce electricity," Bernacchi said. "And agrivoltaics really does bill itself as sort of a middle ground. You can still farm and still get the electricity from the same land."
Agrivoltaic combines solar power and agriculture

articles.title: TIMELINE: Mary Jane Veloso’s case and road to freedom
articles.summary: The pardon granted to Mary Jane Veloso marks the end of a nearly two-decade ordeal that has spanned three presidents and years on death row

items: Mary Jane Veloso, a former overseas Filipino worker, was sentenced to death in Indonesia for drug trafficking in 2010.
She was granted a last-minute reprieve from execution in 2015 and was later transferred to a Philippine prison in 2024.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. granted Veloso absolute pardon on September 24, 2026.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Former overseas Filipino worker (OFW) Mary Jane Veloso left the Philippines for a job in Malaysia in 2010. She instead found herself in Indonesia — behind bars and on death row — after being accused of smuggling drugs.

Sixteen years later, she will soon walk free. This is after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. confirmed on Friday, September 25, that he had granted her absolute pardon for the drug trafficking conviction decided upon by an Indonesian court in 2010.

blocks.caption: Marcos pardons Mary Jane Veloso

blocks.text: Her pardon marks the end of a nearly two-decade ordeal spanning three presidents and years on death row.
Here’s a look back on how her case unfolded:

Veloso returns to the Philippines after prematurely ending her two-year contract as a domestic worker in Dubai. She says it is because she was nearly raped. For the next three months, she attempts to apply for jobs in other countries through her agency, but to no avail.
Maria Cristina Sergio, Veloso’s neighbor in Talavera, Nueva Ecija, offers her a job as a domestic worker in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

Veloso and Sergio arrive in Malaysia, only to find that the job she was promised is no longer available. Both stay in Malaysia for three days, during which Sergio and her boyfriend give Veloso a brand-new suitcase to use plus $500.
She later says that the suitcase seemed heavy, but its compartments were empty. She packs her belongings in the suitcase and leaves for Indonesia.

blocks.caption: The story of Mary Jane Veloso, in her own words

blocks.text: Veloso arrives at the Adisucipto International Airport in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, where authorities find 2.6 kilograms of heroin wrapped in aluminum foil hidden inside the lining of her suitcase. The drugs are later estimated to have a street value of $500,000.
She is arrested for drug trafficking and taken into custody.

Veloso’s parents find out that she has been jailed, weeks after Sergio had assured them that Mary Jane arrived safely in Malaysia. The family confronts Sergio, who tells them to “keep silent, don’t tell anyone, and don’t approach the media” if they want to keep Mary Jane and the rest of their family out of grave danger.

Veloso’s family decides to report her case to the Department of Foreign Affairs and media outlets. They repeatedly request for updates and ask for help from other authorities like the National Bureau of Investigation, Philippine National Police, Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency, Office of the Vice President, and Malacañang.

The trial for Veloso’s case begins in the District Court of Justice of Sleman in Yogyakarta with Indonesian public prosecutor Sri Anggraeni recommending life imprisonment. Veloso is represented by a court-appointed pro bono lawyer apparently recommended by the Indonesian police themselves. (READ: What you should know about the case of Mary Jane Veloso)
The Sleman District Court convicts Veloso of drug trafficking and sentences her to death by firing squad.
The Philippine embassy in Jakarta reportedly files an appeal for Veloso with Yogyakarta’s Appeals Court.
The late former president Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III makes his first attempt to appeal for clemency on behalf of Veloso to then-Indonesian president Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono.
At the time, Indonesia had a moratorium on executions, so the request was not acted upon.

A new Indonesian president, Joko “Jokowi” Widodo, assumes office. Shortly after, he announces that he will start rejecting all clemency requests from drug convicts on death row, citing Indonesia’s illegal drug situation being in a state of emergency.

Jokowi rejects a batch of clemency appeals, including Aquino’s second attempt to appeal for Veloso by seeking a judicial review of her case. The Indonesian Supreme Court rejects this, and Jokowi would later urge the Philippines to respect his country’s laws.
Jokowi goes on his first state visit to the Philippines, during which Aquino raises Veloso’s case. Later that same month, her family visits her in jail in Yogyakarta.
The Sleman District Court holds a two-day trial, where lawyers argue that Veloso deserves a case review because she wasn’t given a capable translator.
The Indonesian Supreme Court rejects the case review request.
The Philippine government attempts to file a second petition for judicial review. Four days later, the Indonesian Supreme Court denies the application.

The DFA later announces that charges have been filed against Veloso’s alleged recruiter Sergio, her boyfriend who allegedly handed Veloso the suitcase where the drugs were found, and an African accomplice.

Veloso’s execution date is set for April 29, 2015. At the same time, global campaigns to stop her execution are mounted. (READ: #SaveMaryJane: A cause worth fighting for during the glorious days of social media)
Sergio voluntarily surrenders to the Nueva Ecija Provincial Police.

Aquino makes a last-minute phone call to then-Indonesian foreign minister Retno Marsudi, asking Indonesia to turn Veloso into a state witness who can help pin down a drug trafficking syndicate, which allegedly includes her recruiters.

Indonesia grants Veloso last-minute reprieve from her death sentence, just 11 hours before she is scheduled to be shot by firing squad. This would allow her to testify against her recruiters, although she would remain in detention.
A few months after then-Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte assumed office, Jokowi reveals to reporters that Duterte told him to “go ahead” if Veloso were to be executed.

Then-presidential spokesperson Ernesto Abella later clarifies Duterte’s statements, saying that he had said, “Follow your own laws, I will not interfere.” (READ: Duterte said he will not interfere with Indonesian laws – Palace)
Veloso’s recruiters are found guilty of illegal recruitment and life imprisonment. This is separate from the trafficking case pending in Indonesia.
After more than 14 years in detention, Veloso is allowed to return to the Philippines, as Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto agrees to transfer her case back home.

Indonesia also gives President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. the discretion to grant Veloso clemency. While this means she is spared from death row — since the Philippines has no such penalty — she could not walk free just yet. (READ: Once Mary Jane Veloso returns, no release yet, but safe from death penalty)

Veloso arrives in Manila after 14 years away from home, but is then detained at the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong City. Despite pleas for her freedom from advocates and supporters, Marcos says he would leave the decision on clemency requests to legal experts.
The embattled OFW would remain behind bars for nearly two more years.

blocks.caption: [DOCUMENTARY] Mary Jane Veloso: So close, yet so far from home

blocks.text: Marcos confirms that he granted Veloso absolute pardon the day before. It is a form of executive clemency granted after conviction and extinguishes the person’s criminal liability from the case. The Parole and Probation Administration says this type of pardon also restores a person’s civil and political rights and cancels the penalty for conviction. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Culinary school, offices shut over alleged unlicensed Australia recruitment
articles.summary: Applicants without experience were allegedly charged P420,000, including about P270,000 for a 12-month culinary program.

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 5:15pm
Ausphin International Institute of Culinary Arts and Business Management in Baguio City is shown in this undated photo.
Ausphin via Google Reviews

MANILA, Philippines — Five offices linked to a culinary school have been shut down over an alleged recruitment scheme that charged applicants as much as P420,000 for training and assistance in securing chef and cook jobs in Australia.

The Department of Migrant Workers on Friday, September 25, implemented a final closure order against Ausphin International Institute of Culinary Arts and Business Management and related operations in Baguio City, Pasig City and Mandaluyong City.

DMW Migrant Workers Protection Bureau head Rommel Abbang said the agency found that the company was allegedly recruiting chefs and cooks for jobs in Australia without the required recruitment license.

"We have closed down Ausphin businesses composed of three divisions after we received a report that they are doing recruitment activities for chefs and cooks with a promised salary of PHP200,000 to PHP250,000," Abbang said during the Baguio operation, as reported by the Philippine News Agency.
Applicants without experience were allegedly asked to pay about P420,000, while those with experience were charged P95,000, according to the DMW.

DMW-Cordillera Regional Director Cheryl Daytec Yangot said the P420,000 payment included about P270,000 in tuition for a 12-month culinary program, plus additional fees for assistance in finding jobs in Australia.
The operation covered Ausphin's culinary school, consultancy and recruitment businesses.
Abbang said the DMW conducted three surveillance operations before finding that the recruitment activities were being carried out without the required license.
All five offices were shut down simultaneously Friday.
'They will not open again'

Ausphin International Institute-Culinary Arts and Business Management Inc. was incorporated on Nov. 16, 2017, according to a Securities and Exchange Commission certification displayed at the facility.
"This is a final closure order and they will not open again," Abbang said.
The DMW will recommend that the Baguio City government cancel the school's business permit and ask the SEC to cancel the company's registration.
The agency will also file criminal complaints for alleged illegal recruitment against the company's incorporators, officers and other individuals allegedly involved in the operations.
Yangot urged students who paid fees after being promised jobs in Australia to file complaints with the DMW.
"We are urging them to complain and we are assisting them to the fullest," she said.
Yangot said DMW lawyers and the Integrated Bar of the Philippines would provide legal assistance in pursuing the cases.
She also urged Filipinos planning to work overseas to verify whether recruitment agencies are licensed and to carefully assess employment pathways offered to them.
"We have zero tolerance, so if you are conducting recruitment activities, please be mindful that you have to secure a license from DMW," Abbang said.

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 25, 2026 5:09pm
The Senate minority bloc will continue participating in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano said Friday.

“Wala naman kaming indication na hindi mag-aattend (There is no indication among us that we will not attend the impeachment trial). It’s our constitutional duty to be part of the impeachment court,” Cayetano said.

“At [ang] fairness ay napaka-importante. Kung tatanungin ninyo kung nagluluksa pa kami, siyempre, kasi we really feel that kung may reinterpretation doon, dapat ang Supreme Court. And we think apektado ang fairness pagka sa gitna ng trial. Having said that, there's a process. [And] so far, wala pa namang pag-uusap na hindi magpa-participate,” he added.

(Fairness is very important. And if you will ask us if we are still mourning over it, of course we are, because we really feel that it should be the Supreme Court to interpret it. And we think fairness is affected if it is done in the middle of the trial. Having said that, there's a process , and there's no talk about us not participating.)
For his part, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said he "has not heard of" the rumored boycott.
“Well, wala naman akong naririnig na ganyan (I did not hear anything of that sort),” Gatchalian said in a chance interview.

On Wednesday, the Senate impeachment court voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."

Thirteen senator-judges, including minority member Mark Villar, voted in favor of the motion put forward by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought reconsideration of the July 6 ruling after some senators became unavailable to participate in the impeachment trial.
Six senator-judges, including Cayetano, did not participate in the voting.
Article 11, Section 6 of the Constitution does not state a number and instead reads "No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate.”
At the same time, the said constitutional provision states that "The Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment."
Cayetano said Villar’s vote in favor the new basis of the threshold does not mean the latter is breaking away from the minority bloc.

“We’re working, and there is no animosity among seven of us in the minority. Of course, we long na mabuo pa rin 'yung 11, but ‘yun nga, four of our colleagues are facing different challenges,” he said.
(We want for all of us 11 to be complete.)
“Pero walang napag-uusapan na, anong next, anong boycott, anong ganyan, o anong sinabi 'yung defense,” Cayetano added.
(There are no talks of what's next, if there will be a boycott, or what did the defense say.) —with Sandra Aguinaldo/AOL, GMA News

articles.title: N.S. lawyers have faced ‘racial double standard’ in how they are disciplined, report finds
articles.summary: Report from Human Rights Commission was spurred by complaint from Lyle Howe, a Black Halifax defence lawyer who was disbarred in 2017

image.caption: A report from the Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission was spurred by complaint from Lyle Howe, a Black Halifax defence lawyer who was disbarred in 2017. (CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New
Report from Human Rights Commission was spurred by complaint from Lyle Howe, a Black Halifax defence lawyer who was disbarred in 2017
Lyle Howe was disbarred in 2017, and has argued for years he is the victim of systemic racism

A report from the Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission says the organization that regulates the province’s legal profession has a “racial double standard” when it comes to disciplining lawyers, including in the case of Lyle Howe, a Black lawyer who was disbarred in 2017.

Howe has argued for years that he is a victim of systemic racism. The former Halifax defence lawyer filed complaints against the Nova Scotia Barristers’ Society with the human rights commission, and an investigator’s report in August 2025 concluded there is merit to his claims.

“The evidence indicates that white lawyers often received more lenient consequences for serious misconduct. Conversely, Black and racialized lawyers faced harsher penalties even for comparable or lesser infractions,” the report reads.
The report recommended the issue be referred to a full board of inquiry.
In February, the chief judge of the Nova Scotia Provincial Court, Perry Borden, named a three-member panel to conduct hearings.

Ordinarily, the process leading up to a board of inquiry is confidential, as is the human rights commission report. But the barristers’ society has asked for a judicial review of the decision to order a hearing.
As part of that review process, the investigator’s report has become a matter of public record.
The findings in her report were welcome news to Howe.

“She found that not only was I discriminated against in the fashion that I described but she went in and investigated in a way that I wouldn't have been able to in terms of looking at how other Black lawyers were dealt with for the last 25 years,” Howe said in an interview earlier this month.

Howe was disbarred by a disciplinary committee of the Nova Scotia Barristers' Society after he was found guilty of professional misconduct and professional incompetence following a 60-day hearing. The panel ruled that complaints against Howe were credible. The complaints alleged Howe scheduled himself to be in two or more courts at the same time, poorly documented his clients' files and provided poor quality of service.
The report compared the treatment Howe received from the society with how it dealt with other – mostly white – lawyers.

In particular, the report considered how the society dealt with prominent Cape Breton defence lawyer Nash Brogan. While Howe was disbarred and is still not allowed to practise law, Brogan received a six-month suspension after a disciplinary panel of the society found him guilty of misconduct and incompetence.
The investigator canvassed more than 60 disciplinary cases from 2000 to 2023. The sanctions against Howe were among the harshest of them all.
Howe is accusing the barristers’ society of being hypocritical, asserting that their position toward him is in stark contrast to their reaction to the Ruck report.
Two years ago, Halifax lawyer and former ombudsman Douglas Ruck produced a report, “Regaining Trust,” which contained 21 recommendations for tackling racism in the Nova Scotia justice system.
“The bar society themselves said, in 2024, we accept all of the recommendations, including the recommendation to go back and look at how Black lawyers were treated,” Howe said.

“And yet they have an opportunity through the human rights commission who's the very body that's designed to look into something like this, allegations of discrimination, and instead of accepting that and saying, well, we're going to examine our processes and see if they were fair, they're fighting it every way they can, they're trying to prevent me from having a board of inquiry.”

In a statement to CBC News earlier this month, Jennifer Pink, interim executive director of the barristers’ society, said “The NSBS vigorously contends that the NSHRC's decision was unreasonable and emerged from a flawed decision-making process on multiple grounds, as detailed in the Society’s Notice for Judicial Review filed with the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia on March 4, 2026.”
Pink goes on to note in her statement that Howe’s allegations of racial bias have been tested in the courts.
“Nova Scotia’s highest court found no evidence to support his allegations,” Pink wrote.

“Further, it concluded that ‘the Ruck Report provides no basis for suggesting that Mr. Howe’s disbarment was marred by systemic racism’. Subsequent applications by Mr. Howe for Leave to Appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada were denied.”
But Howe said the focus of the human rights commission is very different from the focus applied by the various courts.
“Now, if we go in front of a human rights commission, the focal point is the bar society discriminated against me,” Howe said.

“So they might try to say Lyle's done all these horrible things, that's fine, but that's in the background and we can't disbar Lyle, it's already been done. So all we can do now is look at your actions, the bar society's actions.”
He says an aspect of his past looms over his battles with the society. In 2014, Howe was convicted of sexual assault in a high-profile jury trial.

While the conviction was overturned on appeal, “There's no question in my mind that their [the disciplinary panel’s] image of me was tainted by the charges that I just beat before I went into this disciplinary proceeding,” Howe said.
“Anybody would be tainted by that.”
He said he still encounters people who assume he was disbarred because of the sexual assault allegation.
As he waits for the court to rule on the society’s request for a judicial review, Howe is somewhat philosophical.

“I'll never be made whole; we're never going to get the years back, I've been out of practice for 10 years,” he said. “The trajectory that my career would have been on had it not been for discrimination, we're never going to fix that. I'm never going to be compensated for what I've lost and I know that.”
But he said if his fight brings about change so Black lawyers in the future don’t face the same obstacles, it would be worth it.
He has a personal stake in that outcome beyond his own story: one of his three sons is considering going to law school.

“I tell him that he shouldn't be a lawyer, he should probably be a scientist or a doctor maybe. But with two parents that are lawyers, I feel like he probably knows that he's got one foot in the door already and, you know, it's scary for me because to know that what I've gone through is one thing but I don't want anyone else to suffer the way that I did.”

articles.title: P.E.I. woman who lost nearly $10K in bitcoin scam wants bank to reimburse her money
articles.summary: Binh Tran has spent the last six months trying to get her money back after falling victim to a scam call.

image.caption: A statement from TD Bank says it understands that it can be 'distressing to be impacted by a scam.' (Ken Linton/CBC)

blocks.text: PEI
Binh Tran has spent the last six months trying to get her money back after falling victim to a scam call.
Binh Tran searched caller's number and found it was the same as on the bank's website
Woman who lost almost $10K in bitcoin scam says banks 'don't care about the customer'
One morning in March, she answered a call from someone claiming to be from TD Bank's fraud prevention department who told her she was needed for an investigation.
"He told me that I … need to withdraw my money for safety," she said.
She was told to stay on the phone while she entered the bank. She withdrew money through a teller and later deposited it into a bitcoin machine for verification.
She felt something was wrong, but she searched online and found the number the scammer used was the same as what was listed on the bank's website, leading her to believe the call was real.
In total, she lost $9,800. Earlier this month, she was informed by TD Bank that she would not be reimbursed.
"I think that the TD Bank, they didn't do anything for investigation," she said.
"They don't care about a customer. They don't care about a customer loss."

items: P.E.I. couple says their kids' RESP is in limbo because the bank altered their last name
Policy requiring P.E.I. seniors to produce bank statements will be changed, minister says

blocks.text: In a statement, TD Bank declined to comment on details of specific cases and said it understands it can be "distressing" to fall victim to a scam. The bank said it takes reports of fraud "very seriously."
"I can confirm TD thoroughly reviewed this matter, shared our findings with Binh, and explained to her the rationale behind our decision," a spokesperson wrote in the statement.
"Helping protect our clients remains a top priority. We have multiple layers of security, monitoring and customer education in place."

TD offered tips to protect against fraud, including not trusting unsolicited calls and not assuming a phone number is legitimate. It also noted that TD "will never ask" a customer for assistance with an investigation or request passwords or one-time security codes sent to mobile devices or email.
The issue for Tran lies with a form she signed when withdrawing the money with the teller, which takes responsibility off of TD Bank to reimburse her money.

It reads that the bank "has warned me that fraudsters may ask their victims to purchase gift cards or bitcoin," and that the customer confirmed that the withdrawal was made of their "own free will, without any coercion or pressure from a third party."
Tran also got police involved, speaking with an officer and filing a report. However, she is not sure how the investigation is progressing.

She said she doesn't agree with TD and plans to appeal the bank's decision to the federal banking ombudsman, noting she took the care to check that the bank's phone number was correct and that she had no reason not to trust it.
"I just work at a Superstore at [a] part-time job, so this is a huge amount. This is my retirement nest, so I cannot lose that amount," she said.
"I just want my money back to my account. It's not easy."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Lucas McInnis is a journalist at CBC Prince Edward Island. He can be reached at lucas.mcinnis@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Padilla appears at DOJ, yet to answer obstruction rap over Dela Rosa's escape
articles.summary: Padilla and his co-respondents have yet to submit their counter-affidavits.

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 4:57pm

Sen. Robin Padilla arrives at the Department of Justice on September 25, 2026, for the preliminary investigation into an obstruction of justice complaint over his alleged role in Sen. Bato Dela Rosa's escape.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Robin Padilla appeared before the Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday, September 25, for the first hearing in the preliminary investigation of an obstruction of justice complaint alleging that he helped Sen. Bato dela Rosa evade arrest.

Padilla and his co-respondents, however, have yet to submit their counter-affidavits as the complainant still has additional documents to provide, according to lawyer Jimmy Bondoc, one of their counsels.
"Kung ano po ang sinasabe ng batas, 'yan po ay susundin natin," Padilla told reporters in an ambush interview. ("Whatever the law says, we will follow.")
Padilla declined to give further details about the hearing.
Bondoc said there were still matters that needed clarification because some submissions from the complainant were incomplete.
"May mga nililinaw pa po dahil may mga konti pang submissions na kulang po from the other side," Bondoc said. "We are in the process of asking for a copy of a complaint," he added.
Lawyer Ferdinand Topacio said the next preliminary investigation hearing is set for November 12.
The complainant, the Philippine National Police-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (PNP-CIDG), has until October 9 to submit additional documents, according to Topacio.

The DOJ had earlier subpoenaed Padilla and his co-respondents over the obstruction complaint and stressed that the issuance of a subpoena is not a finding of guilt. The preliminary investigation will determine whether there is sufficient basis to file a case in court.
Complaint over Dela Rosa's evasion

The complaint stems from allegations that Padilla and others helped Dela Rosa evade authorities after he left the Senate compound in the early hours of May 14, following a shooting incident at the Senate the previous night.

The International Criminal Court had issued a warrant for Dela Rosa, who remains at large, for crimes against humanity of murder for heading the Philippine National Police in the conduct of the Duterte administration's deadly war on drugs.
Philippine authorities said video footage showed Dela Rosa leaving the Senate premises and entering a Toyota Fortuner registered to Padilla.
Padilla has acknowledged that Dela Rosa rode in his vehicle as they left the Senate, but he has disputed the accusation that he helped the senator evade arrest.
The PNP-CIDG filed the obstruction complaint with the DOJ on May 28.
A separate complaint related to Dela Rosa's departure from the Senate was also filed before the Office of the Ombudsman, involving other officials and individuals.

articles.title: OVP says no funds lost after COA flags documentation deficiencies
articles.summary: After the Commission on Audit (COA) flagged the Office of the Vice President (OVP) for deficient documentation involving P168 million in 2025, the latter maintained that there were no funds lost and…

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 4:53pm

After the Commission on Audit (COA) flagged the Office of the Vice President (OVP) for deficient documentation involving P168 million in 2025, the latter maintained that there were no funds lost and that any discrepancy was due to “changes in circumstances."

In its report on the 2025 Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund, COA said that there were inconsistencies between the Office’s situational reports, deviations from approved mission orders, and deficiencies in records.

“The discrepancies arose from changes in circumstances and field conditions that became apparent as the operations were carried out. No funds were lost, and all funds are accounted for,” the OVP said.

“The relief operations were actually carried out, and the beneficiaries were recorded and validated based on the available supporting documents and field records submitted to the COA Audit Team,” they added.

The OVP said that the matter raised by COA was regarding deficiencies in “pre-operation documentary requirements” that the Office itself required for internal procedures. They did not fail to comply with any requirements mandated by the law or the COA.

“The OVP continues to strengthen its processes for documentation, validation, and monitoring to ensure that the records of every operation are complete and in order, especially during emergency responses and calamities,” the Office added.

COA flagged several types of deficiencies in the OVP. For example, COA found that there was a difference between the situational reports prepared by the OVP when compared with those of other concerned agencies and local government units.

The Commission also flagged 24 relief operations involving ng P39.01 million worth of welfare goods that deviated from approved mission orders. This was done without documented approval. State auditors also found that there were eight mission orders without specific target beneficiaries—in total, they covered P84.12 million.
The lack of clear beneficiaries made it difficult to determine the quantity of relief goods requested and distributed, according to the COA. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Meet the new cornerstone investors lining up for GCash’s record IPO
articles.summary: From the world's biggest asset manager to the World Bank's private sector investment arm, GCash has already secured about P36.5 billion in cornerstone commitments ahead of its October 6-12 IPO offer…

blocks.text: From the world's biggest asset manager to the World Bank's private sector investment arm, GCash has already secured about P36.5 billion in cornerstone commitments ahead of its October 6-12 IPO offer period
MANILA, Philippines – More than 20 global and local institutions have already lined up to buy into GCash even before its record-setting initial public offering (IPO) opens to ordinary investors.
Mynt, the parent company of GCash, said its cornerstone investors include some of the biggest names in global asset management. Among the most notable global investors are:

Together, the cornerstone investors have committed around P36.5 billion, according to Mynt’s preliminary prospectus. Mynt said the commitments would cover approximately the entire institutional tranche, subject to any reallocation.

blocks.caption: For GCash’s early private equity backers, record IPO will be ultimate payday

blocks.text: Cornerstone investors are large institutions that agree in advance to buy shares in an IPO, giving an issuer a ready pool of demand before the public offer begins.

The biggest name on the list by sheer scale is BlackRock. The New York-listed investment giant had $15.3 trillion (P959.85 trillion) in assets under management as of end-June 2026, making it the world’s largest asset manager. Note though that the expected buyers are certain funds and separately managed accounts run by BlackRock subsidiaries, rather than BlackRock itself.

GCash is also not BlackRock’s first time coming into a company at the IPO stage. BlackRock-managed funds and accounts were named as a cornerstone investor in trading platform eToro’s 2025 listing, indicating interest in buying up to $100 million (P6.27 billion) of shares at the IPO price.

Another heavyweight is Capital Research and Management Company, part of Capital Group, which manages more than $3.6 trillion (P225.85 trillion). A Capital Group investment division was also among the cornerstone investors in US electric vehicle maker Rivian’s blockbuster 2021 IPO. Rivian’s cornerstone group, which also included Amazon and T. Rowe Price, indicated interest in buying as much as $5 billion (P313.68 billion) of stock at the IPO price. Rivian ultimately raised nearly $12 billion and its shares jumped about 29% on their first trading day.

T. Rowe Price, which managed around $1.9 trillion (P119.20 trillion) as of end-August, has played the same role in an even more recognizable listing. It committed up to €750 million (P53.48 billion) as a cornerstone investor in German luxury sports car manufacturer Porsche’s 2022 IPO. Porsche later described the listing as the largest IPO ever carried out in Europe, with a market capitalization of around €78 billion (P5.56 trillion) at its opening price.
Perhaps the most interesting incoming investor from a Philippine fintech perspective is the International Finance Corporation, the private sector arm of the World Bank Group.

GCash is not IFC’s first exposure to the local digital finance race. In 2022, IFC and two IFC-managed funds invested up to $18.5 million (P1.16 billion) in Voyager Innovations, the company behind rival Maya, as part of a funding round meant to support its expansion into digital banking. That means IFC is entering GCash as a cornerstone investor after already backing one of its closest competitors in the Philippine fintech market.
On the domestic side, Mynt named ATRAM Trust, BPI Asset Management and Trust, China Bank Capital, Metrobank’s Trust Banking Group, Philequity Management, and RCBC Capital.

The new investors are arriving just as several of GCash’s early private equity backers prepare to sell down their stakes through the IPO. Bow Wave Capital, Warburg Pincus, Insight Partners, and LGVP are among the existing shareholders using the listing as a partial exit.

Mynt is expected to set the final offer price on October 1, ahead of the October 6 to 12 offer period and its targeted October 20 debut on the Philippine Stock Exchange under the ticker GCASH. – Rappler.com
$1 = P62.6190, €1 = P71.3043 based on the September 24, 2026 reference exchange rates of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas

articles.title: Pacquiao, other officials visit Pag-asa Island, face Chinese radio challenge
articles.summary: Several government officials visited Pag-asa Island in the West Philippine Sea on Friday as part of the observance of Maritime and Archipelagic Nation Awareness Month.

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 4:44pm
Several government officials visited Pag-asa Island in the West Philippine Sea on Friday as part of the observance of Maritime and Archipelagic Nation Awareness Month.
According to a report by Jonathan Andal on GTV’s Balitanghali the delegation included newly appointed National Anti-Poverty Commission (NAPC) lead convenor Manny Pacquiao.
He was joined by Presidential Adviser for Maritime Concerns Andres Centino and Representatives Keith Flores and Jesus Marquez.
The officials were set to distribute assistance to residents and assess the needs of the island community.
Flores said they wanted to personally see the situation in Pag-asa Island, particularly as Congress works on next year’s national budget.
Pacquiao brought P500,000 worth of assistance from the NAPC.
Kalayaan Mayor Billy Alindogan said the island has around 450 residents, including more than 100 students up to Grade 12 and over 30 fishermen.
He said the population continues to grow as some residents from mainland Palawan choose to settle on the island.

Among the local government's requests are a new municipal building, an improved drainage system, typhoon-resilient housing, more water filtration facilities, and enough rice stocks to last three months.
Alindogan said seawater can overflow onto parts of the island during strong storms, highlighting the need for improved drainage and more resilient infrastructure.

The National Mapping and Resource Information Authority (NAMRIA) also provided an updated map of Pag-asa Island, containing information on the depth of surrounding waters and Filipino names for features in the West Philippine Sea.
New infrastructure has been completed on the island, including a hangar and terminal at the airport.
Flores said the Philippine delegation encountered challenges during their flight to Pag-asa Island, which he attributed to China.
Despite the reported challenges, Flores said the Philippine pilots stood their ground and were able to safely land on the island.—Joviland Rita/LDF, GMA News

blocks.text: September 25, 2026
Germany's Heidenau bans new Stolpersteine dedicated to victims of Holocaust

The town of Heidenau, near Dresden, has banned new Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) on the public streets, with the center-right CDU and the far-right AfD voting together to curb the installation of new memorial plaques bearing the names of Holocaust victims.

The city's administration urged against the motion. The initiators, however, argued that placing the plaques in the street leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims." They suggested honoring Holocaust victims at one of the city's cemeteries instead.
Stumbling stones — against forgetting

With the local branch of Friedrich Merz's CDU joining forces with the AfD to pass the motion, it has also raised questions about the political "firewall" against the far right pledged by mainstream German parties.
The International Auschwitz Committee described the CDU support as scandalous.

"This is a transparent and despicable attempt to drive Nazi victims in Heidenau out of the city once again and dispose of them where, according to the AfD, their memory has belonged a long time ago — at the cemetery," said the organization's Executive Vice President Christoph Heubner.

articles.title: Lawyer petitions SC to void Senate impeachment court ruling on threshold
articles.summary: Another lawyer has filed a petition before the Supreme Court (SC), asking it to void the Senate impeachment court"s recent ruling that excluded non-participant senator-judges in computing the…

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 4:20pm

Another lawyer has filed a petition before the Supreme Court (SC), asking it to void the Senate impeachment court’s recent ruling that excluded non-participant senator-judges in computing the threshold needed for Vice President Sara Duterte’s conviction.
This is the second petition challenging the voting threshold decided on September 23, 2026.

In a 112-page petition for certiorari and prohibition filed on Friday, Atty. Ernesto Francisco Jr. prayed for a Status Quo Ante Order (SQAO) to reverse the changes that took effect after the impeachment court’s ruling.

“It is most respectfully prayed that upon the filing of this Petition, a Status Quo Ante Order be issued directing the parties to maintain the last actual, peaceable and uncontested state of affairs that existed before the present controversy,” the petition’s prayer read.
“It is further prayed of the Honorable Court that the proceedings conducted on 23 September 2026 that led to the issuance of the Ruling be declared null and void,” it added.

Francisco asked for the SC’s intervention as the final arbiter on the issue, adding that the impeachment court's decision will “surely lead to further division of the Filipino people and likely political chaos and instability.”
He emphasized that an SQAO is an essential measure that must be issued immediately to avoid “grave and irreparable” injurious consequences to the case.

Former Executive Secretary Vic Rodriguez also previously asked the High Court to declare the impeachment court’s September 23 ruling null and void, arguing that the Constitution sets the voting threshold at two-thirds of all members of the Senate, which should be 16 if all 24 senators are counted.

On Wednesday, 13 senator-judges voted in favor of the motion to base the two-thirds conviction vote on the number of senators who are "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."
Senator Francis Escudero, the impeachment court presiding officer, said that under this rule, the members excluded from the vote count are those:

articles.summary: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government has passed new school rules capping the number of students who don't speak fluent Italian and banning face coverings.

image.caption: Meloni said the burqa ban was 'a matter of security' Image: Alessandra Tarantino/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Italy's conservative government on Thursday approved a new decree banning face-covering Islamic veils — including burqas and niqabs — in schools and putting a limit on the number of students with a poor command of the Italian language in each classroom.

Italian Prime Minister, Giorgia Meloni, called her Cabinet's measures "tools of common sense that do not divide," adding that they will help integration by avoiding what the right-wing leader called "ghetto classes."
She went on to say the rules would lead to all students receiving the "same opportunities."

Opposition parties and other critics have denounced the move by Meloni's government, with some calling it a "witch hunt” and others accusing the government of turning immigration into more of a political issue ahead of next year's general election.
What do Italy's new school rules entail?
The measures take effect right away but still require parliamentary approval within 60 days. Meloni's coalition currently holds a majority in the country's legislature.
Here is what the decree includes:

items: A per-classroom cap of 30% for foreign students who lack sufficient proficiency in Italian
In primary schools, the limit applies to pupils without Italian citizenship who were not born in Italy or did not attend at least two years of preschool
In lower and upper secondary schools, the same limit applies to students without Italian citizenship who have not attended the country's school system for at least three years
Failure to comply with the decree is punishable by a fine of up to €1,000 euros ($1,140)

blocks.text: Face-coverings banned in schools
The decree bans burqas and niqabs in schools but will continue to allow hijabs.
Meloni said the burqa ban was "a matter of security."

"When a woman — or worse, a young girl — is forced to cover her face, she is being denied fundamental rights and the very integration that is so often loudly championed," Meloni was quoted as saying in a television interview.
Italian Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the decree would affect about 1,000 classrooms, which come up to 0.3% of the nationwide tally.
According to official data, pupils without Italian citizenship comprised 11.2% of Italy's school population from 2022 to 2023, while classes with over 30% foreign students stood at 7.6% of the total.
What do critics say?
Opponents of the decree are worried that the new measure could force students to attend schools far from the neighborhoods where they live.
Reports have also highlighted concerns among school authorities regarding how the rules would work in areas with large migrant populations.

Independent child rights organization Save the Children had on Wednesday called on the Italian government to weigh the measure "with the utmost political responsibility,” adding that it risked creating discriminatory effects.
"Such a criterion would create ‘first-class' and 'second-class' students," the organization said in its statement.
Meanwhile, opposition leader Elly Schlein railed against the decree, accusing Meloni's government of "a new witch hunt at the expense of children."
Meloni is at the head of the most right-wing government that Italy has seen since World War II.
