articles.title: Wheelchair user says ‘discriminatory’ Habs policy forced him to beg for tickets
articles.summary: Unlike other customers who can purchase Habs tickets online, customers who want reduced-mobility seating have to call or go in-person to the Bell Centre's ticket office. But this year, Joey Racanelli…

image.caption: Joey Racanelli has bought Habs tickets in the reduced mobility section at the Bell Centre for years. This year, he was told a new policy limited him to one game per season. (Louis-Marie Philidor/CBC)

blocks.text: With the Habs falling just shy of reaching the Stanley Cup final last spring, Joey Racanelli, like most fans, couldn’t wait to buy tickets for the upcoming season.
But when single-game tickets went on sale in early September, his excitement was short-lived.

As a wheelchair user, he buys tickets in the Bell Centre’s accessible seating section. He typically goes to four or five games a season. But without warning, he says the Canadiens quietly changed their policy on reduced mobility seats, limiting him to one match for the entire season.
“I don't think it's their goal,” he added, “but it certainly feels discriminatory.”
Unlike other customers who can purchase tickets online, customers who want reduced mobility seating don’t have that option. They have to call or go in person to the Bell Centre ticket office.

Racanelli described the experience on the phone with the agent as he tried to get to the bottom of why his access was being restricted as embarrassing: “I basically had to beg for more tickets and I still couldn’t get them.”

Steven Laperrière, the general manager of the disability advocacy group Regroupement des activistes pour l'inclusion au Québec (RAPLIQ), says setting different limits to the number of tickets a disabled person can buy could amount to a violation of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
“You cannot discriminate against persons because of their handicap, you cannot do that.” Laperrière said.
He also takes issue with the policy at large. “Why would a person be only allowed to have only one game per season? We’re in a free country, right?”
CBC confirmed through several other Habs fans who use wheelchairs that Racanelli's experience was not isolated.
Quebec wheelchair user says new ticket policy at Habs home games feels ‘discriminatory’
Paying the price for possible system abuse
At the time, Racanelli asked the ticket agent why the policy had changed.
“It felt like [they thought] I was trying to abuse the system, which obviously I was not. I was just trying to get my tickets,” said Racanelli.
Laperrière says he understands it can be challenging for event managers to make sure the accessible seats are being used properly.
At the Bell Centre, Habs tickets in the reduced mobility section come at a much lower price than the other seats around them, which could tempt people to try and game the system.

“There will still be abuse, for sure. But why do people with disabilities have to pay the price and be limited in their ability to go see the Habs games because you can’t manage that properly?” he asks.

items: Concerns for Montrealers with reduced mobility as streets close for major cycling races
Para hockey organizers fear loss of Montreal arena parking lot will make access difficult

blocks.text: People with invisible disabilities like deafness, low vision or intellectual disabilities also have the right to use the accessible and reduced mobility section.
“I get it, it can be tough and you cannot prevent everything,” Laperrière says, “but no constraints is worth limiting the freedom of people with disabilities.”

CBC’s investigation found no evidence that the ticket policy change was disclosed publicly or communicated in any way to longtime users of the accessible and reduced mobility section at the Bell Centre prior to them calling to reserve tickets.
Laperrière says regardless of why the team changed their policy, the lack of communication with users is inexcusable.
“[Groupe CH] is a big corporation, they do business everywhere. They should know better. And to me, that they’re not putting it online is a lack of transparency, and I think we can understand why.”

Laperrière also phoned the ticket office himself to ask for clarification on the policy, which he recorded. He shared that conversation and a recording from another wheelchair user with CBC. In it, the ticket agent confirms they can only buy tickets for one match per season.

Racanelli says in addition to asking for answers on the phone, he emailed Groupe CH and reached out to the Montreal Canadiens on social media regarding the ticketing policy changes. He did not receive a response.
Team says policy applied to all fans, was temporary
The Montreal Canadiens and Groupe CH declined to be interviewed for this story.
In a statement, the club says that due to high demand, purchases were limited to one game per person, but added that the policy applied to all fans, not just those with reduced mobility.
It added that the policy was only in effect for a limited time, and now that the initial sales period is over, single-game tickets can be purchased — subject to availability.
However, even if the policy was applied to all fans during the limited period, the number of tickets available per client appeared to differ.
When single-game tickets came on sale in early September, customers buying through Ticketmaster were limited to four seats per purchase.

items: Ticket system for accessible seats fails disabled fans, wheelchair user says | Go Public

blocks.text: Users of the reduced mobility section were only allowed to purchase the equivalent of two tickets — one for themselves and one for the person accompanying them.

For years, customers who wanted reduced mobility seating had to call or go in person to the ticketing office. That briefly changed last season, when the team moved everything to Ticketmaster. But it reverted to the old system this year.
CBC asked Groupe CH why it moved away from online sales after one year, and if or how it communicated the policy to customers in advance, but it did not provide an answer.
Racanelli says his frustration over the situation grew when he went online and saw other fans on social media talking about all the tickets they acquired to multiple games this season.
Based on his experience, there were no guardrails preventing others from buying tickets to multiple games online.

Racanelli was surprised to learn the one-ticket policy was temporary because at no point did the ticketing agent explain that to him when he asked for details. CBC can confirm that others who inquired were also not told the policy was meant to be temporary.
Despite what wheelchair users were told on the phone, Groupe CH said in its statement “no limits have been placed on the number of games a person with reduced mobility may attend during the season.”
Limited reduced mobility seats in Canadian NHL arenas
How users access the reduced mobility section at other Canadian NHL cities varies.
In Ottawa, Toronto and Winnipeg, wheelchair users can buy their tickets online through Ticketmaster.
Spaces in NHL arenas are limited. According to the Montreal Canadiens website, there are only 58 wheelchair-accessible seats available per game at the Bell Centre.
The Ottawa Senators say the Canadian Tire Centre has 140 accessible seats available.
Winnipeg has accessible spaces across 11 sections in the Canada Life Centre for Jets games, but it’s unclear how many seats are available per game.
The Toronto Maple Leafs say it is against company policy to disclose how many seats it offers wheelchair users each game at Scotiabank Arena.

The Calgary Flames, Edmonton Oilers and Vancouver Canucks did not respond to CBC’s request for information concerning how access to the accessible and reduced mobility section operates in their arenas.
Racanelli says he understands there are significant challenges in managing the access to reduced-mobility sections at the Bell Centre.
He adds that his experiences at the arena and with the staff are always first-class, but the ticket process has been so challenging this year that he’s questioning going back.

articles.title: Mamdani's populist style is all over the Toronto election race
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani's 2025 mayoral campaign put a spotlight on cost of living issues and was characterized by colourful messaging, snappy social media videos and a where-there’s-a-will-there’s-a-way…

blocks.text: The Mamdani blueprint: How Toronto candidates are chasing young voters
Last fall, the world watched as New York City elected a young, progressive candidate — a virtual unknown at the start — as mayor.

Zohran Mamdani's campaign put a spotlight on cost of living issues and was characterized by colourful messaging, snappy social media videos and a where-there’s-a-will-there’s-a-way approach to making changes in New York.
Since his victory, Mamdani has introduced city-run grocery stores, free public child care for two-year-olds and a mayoral office dedicated to protecting workers' rights.
His approach to governance in New York became a sensation — and seems to be an inspiration for many candidates in Toronto’s municipal election, just a month away.
Walk-and-talk, on-the-street social media videos have become a staple for mayoral candidates Chris Alexander, Brad Bradford and incumbent Olivia Chow as a way to explain their platforms.

The style is also extremely popular among councillor candidates. Davenport incumbent Alejandra Bravo posted a video of her shooting hoops to promote more food and drink options in parks. Josh Matlow, the incumbent in Toronto–St. Paul's, made a video on the Eglinton LRT talking about transit policy.

Some candidates have chosen to use colours close to Mamdani’s signature blue, orange and red in their marketing campaigns, while others are using a similar bubbly serif font on their campaign's social media.

Saman Tabasinejad, executive director of third-party political organizing group Progress Toronto, which works to get progressive candidates, including Chow, elected, said Mamdani is a "generational talent" when it comes to communication.
CBC Toronto's election podcast breaks down how candidates keep copying Mamdani:

She said he is able to explain policy ideas in a way that helps voters see a clear path forward to a better city. She’s not surprised Toronto candidates are taking inspiration from Mamdani, but cautioned some candidates may be co-opting his style to promote otherwise clashing platforms.
"If you want to be like Mamdani, that's great," she said. "But you’ve got to be like him in many other ways."
Social media in place of traditional coverage
Chiara Padovani, a progressive candidate in York–South Weston, said Mamdani’s social media videos were a clever workaround given his initial lack of traditional media coverage.
Mamdani, a former state assembly member, was up against Andrew Cuomo, who was previously governor and comes from a political family.
"[Mamdani] wasn't going to be getting mainstream media attention and he didn't let that stop him," Padovani said.

It's something Padovani — who came within 94 votes of beating city council’s longest-standing incumbent, Frances Nunziata, in 2022 — says she can relate to. She says Mamdani's strategy can be applied to city councillor races at a hyperlocal level.
"I think candidates who are challenging a mainstream candidate or a mainstream politician do need to find creative ways to get their message across," she said.

In one of his social media videos, Uthish Ganesh, a history and English teacher and candidate in Scarborough Centre, promised to remove a bus lane along Kennedy Road, saying it creates gridlock for drivers and other commuters.
Scarborough Centre candidate calls for bus lane removal on Kennedy Road:
While the style of the video, right down to the campaign colours, is akin to Mamdani's, the New York mayor’s policies are very pro-transit.
Ganesh told CBC that while some of his politics differ from Mamdani’s, he was inspired by the New York mayor's ability to mobilize voters face-to-face.
"We knocked on doors for months before we posted anything worth watching," he said. "If you make videos first, you're guessing what people care about. If you knock first, you already know."
Winning the ground game

Mamdani had a team of nearly 100,000 volunteers and his success in on-the-street canvassing was a major lift in the campaign. In comparison, Progress Toronto currently has a team of around 3,000 volunteers, according to Tabasinejad.
"He won because of a ground game. He was outspent by quite a bit," said Tabasinejad.

Brian Evans, a politics and public administration professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, said that kind of mobilization is unlikely to happen in Toronto’s mayoral race, because there’s less political polarization here.
Mamdani's campaign "drew the ire of Trump and it drew the ire of the uber, uber wealthy," Evans said. "It's going to be a totally different thing here."
How Zohran Mamdani is reshaping New York’s mayoral race

Chloe Brown, a progressive who ran for mayor in 2022 and 2023 — finishing third and seventh, respectively — is now running for councillor in Etobicoke North. She is up against incumbent Coun. Vincent Crisanti and eight other candidates.

Brown said left-wing voters in Toronto, particularly young ones, like to jump on the bandwagon of an exciting candidate, but fall short when it comes to volunteering in campaigns and even showing up at the polls.
"So you get stuck wanting what New York [has], because you don't put in the effort of New York," she said.
Brown also noted that Toronto already has a progressive mayor in Chow, although some councillors have opted not to adopt her policies in their wards.
"It's not enough to want one Mamdani. You need to want 15 of them," said Brown.
Toronto's progressive mayor
This city copied some of Mamdani’s ideas even before the election races kicked off.
Toronto council has greenlit a city-run grocery store pilot, approved a pitch to hire citizen snow shovellers and moved forward on banning surveillance pricing on groceries.

All three were introduced in New York by Mamdani’s administration. Here in Toronto, it was Chow who pitched the snow shovellers and the surveillance pricing ban, while Anthony Perruzza, incumbent in Humber River–Black Creek, put forward the motion on grocery stores.

Chow also raised taxes for homes over $3 million last year, in a move similar to Mamdani’s tax on luxury second homes. The Toronto and New York mayors also have similar politics on tenant protections and supporting city libraries.

My day in New York continues with a mayors roundtable, and bilateral meetings with @NYCMayor and @jaumecollboni. Meetings with more mayors to follow this afternoon.

We’re exchanging ideas for improving service delivery and affordability for residents. pic.twitter.com/kcNHajUm4U—MayorOliviaChow

Chow and Mamdani’s office have in fact had meetings since he took office, a source in Chow’s office told CBC Toronto. Chow was also in New York this week for a cities summit, co-chaired by Mamdani, and met with him one-on-one.

One key distinction between the Toronto mayoral race and the last New York City vote is that the progressive has the incumbent advantage here, says Tabasinejad, which means Chow's campaign will have different challenges than Mamdani's did.
In any case, the issues that defined the New York mayoral race — housing and affordability — are certainly at play in Toronto's election, Evans says.
"But it will have nowhere near the drama."

articles.title: The 1990s boy band mall tour is back, and this time it's sponsored by Gap
articles.summary: Remember when you could hit up your local suburban mall, catch a show from a pop star next to the food court and buy a new zip-up while you were at it? History is repeating itself. On Tuesday, Gap…

image.caption: Bryan Holden Chan, Recker Eans, Tyler Georgeso, Caden Adamonis and Toby Green of the boy band Just Your Type attend a party in February 2026. The boy band is collaborating with Gap, the company said. (Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images for Universal Music Group)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Remember when you could hit up your local suburban mall, catch a show from a pop star next to the food court and buy a new zip-up while you were at it? History is repeating itself. On Tuesday, Gap announced it was launching a collaboration with emerging boyband Just Your Type for its “fashiontainment platform.”
Gap partnering with Just Your Type for 'fashiontainment' platform
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 25, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago
Remember when you could hit up your local suburban mall, catch a show from a pop star next to the food court and buy a new zip-up while you were at it? History is repeating itself.
On Tuesday, Gap announced it was launching a collaboration with emerging boy band Just Your Type (JYT) in the company's first project for its “fashiontainment platform.”

No, we're not really sure what that is either. According to Gap, the platform "leverages the power of its iconic brands to create content." It says it will co-produce a docuseries about the group’s formation and early journey, design a capsule clothing collection with the five members and create social media content to accompany the project.
Taking a page out of the pop playbook of the 1990s and 2000s, the collaboration will also feature a mall tour across the U.S.
CBC News reached out to Gap about whether the tour will come to Canada, but has not heard back.
The band behind the brand
JYT is a five-member boy band made up of performers Recker Eans, Toby Green, Caden Adamonis, Bryan Chan and Tyler George.
Haven’t heard of JYT? That’s not surprising — the group just released their debut single What U Want at the end of last year, and only have four songs out in total.
But music executives have been betting big on the group from the start.

In January, the group was officially signed by Republic Records in partnership with Grammy-nominated songwriter and producer Freddy Wexler, who developed them. Wexler has worked on hits for artists including Justin Bieber, Blackpink and Ariana Grande.

“From the moment these five kids stood in a room together, I knew we had something special. JYT isn’t a manufactured boy band; they chose each other,” Wexler told UDiscover Music, a Universal Music Group-backed site. “America hasn’t launched a global boy band in decades, and these kids are about to change that.”

With smooth harmonies and a knack for dancing in formation, it seems JYT are being positioned as spiritual successors to boy bands such as NSync and the Backstreet Boys — and potentially the American answer to the tightly choreographed, aesthetically and musically polished groups that have come out of South Korea, such as global K-pop sensation BTS.
Setting the tone

The group may be young, ranging from ages 15 to 17, but most have been working in entertainment for years; the band includes two former touring members of Kidz Bop, and some members have appeared as backup dancers in music videos and in guest roles on TV shows.

The collaboration suggests that Gap is doubling down on attempts to reach Gen Z and Gen Alpha. The company scored a viral ad campaign in 2025 featuring girl group Katseye, who performed a choreographed dance in Gap denim. This followed the hiring of designer Zac Posen to help boost its cultural capital in 2024.

“This campaign demonstrated the power of the playbook in action, featuring trend-right product, amplified by culturally relevant storytelling,” Richard Dickson, Gap CEO, said of the ad on a call with investors about the company's third-quarter results earlier this year. Comparable sales in that quarter rose five per cent, driven by the success of the ad, according to CNBC.
Dickson called the collaboration a “true cultural takeover,” relying on a methodology Gap will continue to build on in the future.
The clothing giant's boy band gamble is a continuation of this, one marketing expert says.

"Inevitably, young people do set the tone in trends like this. So you're not doing this just so that you connect with teenagers and young adults," said Max Valiquette, a communications professional and trends expert. "You're doing this because if they say something is cool or interesting, it does tend to have an impact on older demographics and drive what they purchase, as well. "
Return of the mall tour

Groups like New Kids on the Block, the Backstreet Boys and even pop icons like Britney Spears famously performed in shopping centres when they were starting out, taking advantage of and driving foot traffic to these locations.
It "makes a ton of sense" that Gap would want to revive this tradition, Valiquette said.

"It's turning to a boy band to kind of test whether entertainment can fully move the needle on apparel sales, but not working with an established boy band. It is working with a boy band who are actually not established at all," Valiquette said.
"And it's building Gap while the band gets built. "
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca
With files from CBC's Makda Ghebreslassie

articles.title: AI 'slop' is dominating menus, as some restaurant owners turn to it to save time and money
articles.summary: Diners have taken to social media to share photos of overly-shiny sandwiches and circular shrimp, lamenting the suspected use of AI. But some in the restaurant business say it's helped them reduce…

image.caption: A burger ordered from The Fancy Induced Burger pictured beside an AI-enhanced image of the product, taken at the chain's Waterloo location on Thursday. (James Dunne/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

Diners have taken to social media to share photos of overly-shiny sandwiches and circular shrimp, lamenting the suspected use of AI. But some in the restaurant business say it's helped them reduce costs and save time in a notoriously difficult industry.
AI use could be problem if it misrepresents the product, but false advertising not a big concern, experts say
From cartoonish-looking sandwiches to doughnut-shaped shrimp, AI might be on the menu at your local fast-food restaurant.

Diners have taken to the internet to share photos of sandwich boards and window displays bearing food they say looks rubbery, surreal and seems to be created with artificial intelligence tools — which have made it increasingly easy to generate visuals on the cheap.

"This looks like what aliens would put in a presentation about what Earth food is," a Reddit user captioned in a post accompanied by a picture of a sandwich board with breaded shrimp and gyros with suspiciously geometric textures.
Others described a CNE sandwich they assumed to be AI-generated as "uncanny and nauseating" and "slop."
And for some Toronto customers, these kinds of images aren't just stomach-turning — they take them as a signal of the restaurant's values.
"I feel like it's really inauthentic and it doesn't make me wanna go eat at your restaurant," said Cynthia Lem.
For her, AI-generated imagery raises questions about what the actual food would look like once it arrives, making her wary of any establishments using the technology.
The death of folk graphic design in favor of AI slop across our country's delis is leading to some incredibly Lovecraftian food horrors pic.twitter.com/snDyC675Ei—samfbiddle

While some consumers say these images are ruining their appetites and raising worries about possible misrepresentations of menu items, those in the restaurant business say it's helped them reduce costs in a notoriously difficult industry. And marketing experts say use of the tech isn't necessarily bad if it's done thoughtfully.
Not all AI use created equally

Before taking a single bite, restaurant-goers rely heavily on imagery to dictate what they order, according to business consultant and Schulich School of Business marketing professor David Pullara. And that means businesses relying on heavy-handed AI imagery are taking a big risk.
"Great food photography sells," said Pullara. "So if you're using AI to generate an image that's terrible, it's going to hurt your sales, it's going to hurt your brand."

But while some consumers might object to the use of AI on principle, he thinks the risk of using it to enhance food photography is low if done well — especially if it can help small- and medium-sized businesses manage their costs.

Restaurant businesses face thin margins, often making it difficult to turn a profit. According to Restaurants Canada's most recent survey of some of its members, 41 per cent said they were operating at a loss or just breaking even, with rising fuel costs only exacerbating issues.

items: Canadian restaurants struggling to turn a profit, new report says

blocks.text: Pullara says hiring a professional photographer is expensive, and might be out of budget for a small restaurant business. For that reason, taking a high-resolution photo of food and using an AI application to make small tweaks could create an image worthy of putting on a menu, Pullara says.

"I don't think it's the AI that makes the image unappealing. I think the problem is asking AI for a photo and just not using a common-sense filter about [whether] this actually looks good," Pullara said.
That tweaking of real photos is how the marketing team at The Fancy Induced Burger uses AI.

A marketing manager for the Canadian franchise, Fez Mian, says he'll snap a picture of a burger as it comes out of the kitchen and run it through an AI application like ChatGPT, prompting it to enhance the texture and freshness of menu items. Those images are used across the business — on menus, in-store posters and online.

The company doesn't rely on professional photographers or graphic designers as much these days as a result. That's saved them money and time, as Mian no longer needs to book a photographer, wait for the shoot date and then wait to receive the images before using them in marketing.
"We're not, like, spending endless time planning and scheduling and whatnot," Mian said. "Within … five minutes, 10 minutes it's out the door."
That speed is especially important on social media, Mian says, enabling them to create and post new content more frequently.
Does AI cross the line into false advertising?
For some consumers, the worry is about how the food item that shows up on their plate will compare to the enhanced image on the menu.
AI food pics on restaurant menus are killing customers' appetites
If AI imagery is vastly different from the actual product, Rotman School of Management marketing professor David Soberman says that could be a problem.

"You wanna make your products look good, but you don't want your products to be misleading," Soberman said. If an AI-enhancement makes a steak look like it's an inch thick but the actual product is half the size, for example, that would be a problem.

But the same is true for food imagery enhanced using run-of-the-mill staging and image editing, Soberman says. Both Soberman and Pullara say they don't think AI imagery generally raises the likelihood of misleading consumers, especially since most have come to accept that images on menu boards will look better than the real deal.

"I think people just kind of know that there's going to be some variance between what you're seeing on these professionally shot, produced photos and what you actually can have prepared in the back of the kitchen in two minutes," Pullara said.

At The Fancy Induced Burger, Mian says there's always a human involved in checking the company's AI-enhanced images to make sure no extra ingredients were added in the process that might mislead customers.
Still, Toronto-based food stylist Zoe Rousseau says they think the work they do is more authentic than AI-generated food imagery.

Despite some common misconceptions based on industry standards from decades ago, Rousseau says food staging doesn't involve fake food most of the time. Instead, they take their time to pick the best-looking ingredients, make sure they're perfectly placed, and work with a team of photographers and prop stylists who help achieve a beautiful end product.
Rousseau says they understand why small businesses trying to cut down costs would try AI, but if the generated imagery simply "doesn't look like the food," it won't work to pull customers in.
"I think that restaurateurs are better off taking pictures with their iPhone," Rousseau said.

For that reason, they're not too worried about AI coming for their job. They hope that the backlash to AI menu items might even compel more businesses to invest in stylists and photographers, boosting their industry.
"I can play with texture and I can play with angles," Rousseau said. "Just the freshness of it … the AI can't do that."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.
With files from Lauren Battagello, James Dunne and Nisha Patel

articles.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is heading to the ISS next week
articles.summary: It’s only been six months since Canada's Jeremy Hansen made history by flying around the moon. Now, it’s Joshua Kutryk’s turn to blast off into space.

image.caption: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk holds up his fingers to make the number 13 to mark his launch as part of Crew 13 launch to the International Space Station. Kutryk and four other astronauts are set to launch on Oct. 1. (SpaceX)

blocks.text: Science·New
It’s only been six months since Canada's Jeremy Hansen made history by flying around the moon. Now, it’s Joshua Kutryk’s turn to blast off into space.
'I never, ever, ever … thought that I would have this opportunity to go out on behalf of Canada,' he says
It's only been six months since Canada's Jeremy Hansen made history by flying around the moon. Now, it's Joshua Kutryk's turn to blast off into space.
But he'll be hanging around closer to home and will be in space for far longer, living and working on the International Space Station (ISS) for roughly six months.
"I never, ever, ever, ever … thought that I would have this opportunity to go out on behalf of Canada and do a mission like this," Kutryk said during a press call on Wednesday.
"I dreamt of it. I always dreamt of it and thought it would be the most wonderful experience, but I always viewed it as impossibly hard."
Kutryk, who was born in Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., is an engineer, fighter pilot and test pilot who has flown more than 4,000 hours on more than 40 different aircraft types.
He was chosen alongside Jenni Gibbons in 2017 by the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) in its recruitment program.
Kutryk was initially supposed to launch on Boeing's CST-100 Starliner. However, Boeing has suffered big setbacks, delaying its first crewed mission.
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk gets ready for ISS mission

Instead, he'll be riding on SpaceX's Crew Dragon. Kutryk was initially supposed to launch on Sept. 12, but there was an issue with the spacecraft, so the launch was delayed to Oct. 1. He said he has faith that the vehicle is ready to fly.
While he's packing light, he'll still be bringing some items into space with him.

"I'm bringing many things from different Canadian organizations, universities, public service agencies that I'm affiliated with," Kutryk said. "I'm bringing a lot of Canadian flags. This idea of being Canadian is something that has always resonated with me."

But one thing of particular importance to him is an old pocket watch that travelled from Ukraine to Canada when his family immigrated here. The watch has actually beaten him to the ISS, however. It went up with an earlier supply launch.
Kutryk said the fact that the watch was likely built in the early 1900s, and is now in space, is something special.

"It's just this really important personal memento, but also a really neat metaphor for how much the world can change … because of how we explore," he said. "I plan to keep it pretty close during those six months."
'Can't wait to look out the window'
When asked what he's looking forward to the most, Kutryk said his answer may seem boring.
"The truth is, the answer to that is the simplest one, and that is: I just can't wait to look out the window," he said.

"The six-year-old kid and me, all the way up to the 44-year-old astronaut, husband, every version of a human I've been in between, the thing that I want to do the most is go to the biggest window I can find and just stare at Earth."
The Crew 13 launch, as it's called, will also include NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins, Luke Delaney and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteriatnikov.
It will also be the first space mission for Delaney and Teteriatnikov.
The crew will join several astronauts who are already on station and will conduct several experiments, some of which are Canadian.

items: Alberta astronaut visits Calgary before September blast-off
Kutryk announced as part of a crew heading to the ISS

blocks.text: Kutryk says that, while there may be a lot of of unrest here on Earth, the mission illustrates how united the world can be.
"There's a lot of chaos. There's a lot of challenge, no doubt everywhere, and Canada's right in the middle of some of that," he said.

"For me, when I step into a suit, and I get to see what we're doing in space with all these countries — the United States, Canada, Russia and so many others in between — it separates me from all the bad headlines, and it shows me what we can do, what the future can be."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science. You can send her story ideas at nicole.mortillaro@cbc.ca.

blocks.caption: President Emmanuel Macron speaks during an interview with France 2 and TF1 at the Elysee Presidential Palace, in Paris. Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images

Former president Nicolas Sarkozy said the decision was Macron’s personal choice, adding that he would have attended if he were still in office.

articles.title: Ethiopia: Internet disrupted in Tigray amid conflict escalation
articles.summary: A web monitor reported an internet disruption in northern Ethiopia amid renewed fighting between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the federal government.

image.caption: Tigrayans rushed to buy supplies after renewed fighting between the TPLF militia and the Ethiopian stateImage: AFP

blocks.text: Access to the internet has been disrupted in northern Ethiopia's Tigray region, the web monitor NetBlocks reported on Friday.
The region has been the site of renewed hostilities this week that shattered a 2022 peace deal between Ethiopia and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) militia.
During the 2020-2022 Tigray war, the region was largely cut off from the outside world and hundreds of thousands of people were left in famine-like conditions.
"Confirmed: Network data indicate a subnational disruption in ⁠northern ⁠Ethiopia corresponding to reports of a telecoms blackout in Tigray," NetBlocks said.
The cause of the disruption was not immediately clear.
The Reuters news agency cited Tigray residents saying panic buying left shop shelves empty.
"There is deep fear that banks, telecom networks, electricity and basic goods could be cut off again," a local resident told the AFP news agency, adding that there was "panic in the community."
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict
TPLF offensive sparks fear of return to war

The TPLF took control of regional airports in Tigray earlier this week and also clashed with government forces in the neighboring Afar and Amhara regions. The militia said it was now in "full-blown war" with Addis Ababa.
The group also formed an anti-government alliance with the Fano militia in Amhara and five other armed groups.
In the 2022-2023 war, Fano fought alongside the federal government against the Tigrayan rebels.
The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 and was later sidelined alongside the rise of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

articles.title: Ban on Discord, Reddit lifted after safety compliance
articles.summary: The two platforms reportedly became inaccessible to some users earlier this week after Philippine authorities gave them a 24-hour ultimatum to establish their presence in the country.

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 2:58pm
The logos of Reddit and Discord, two popular online platforms where users can interact, share content and join communities.
Reddit and Discord
MANILA, Philippines — Access to online community platforms Discord and Reddit has been restored after the companies have agree to comply with the safety guidelines set by the Philippine government.
The two platforms reportedly became inaccessible to some users earlier this week after Philippine authorities gave them a 24-hour ultimatum to establish their presence in the country.

In a press release on Friday, September 25, the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) announced that the platforms have formally agreed with the government’s standards amid the ongoing evaluation of children’s online safety.

“The temporary restriction successfully compelled both tech giants to establish binding, operational commitments with the DICT and the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC),” the press release read.
According to DICT, Reddit and Discord committed to establish a “green lane” for local authorities for immediate removal of exploitative materials and channels targeting minors.
Also included in the agreement is the implementation of age-verification systems and close coordination with the country’s cybersecurity agencies.
The agreement prompted the DICT to direct the National Telecommunications Commission (NCT) and internet service providers in the country to restore the access on Reddit and Discord nationwide.

The recent move of the DICT and CICC came following the deadly school shooting incident in South Cotabato on September 18, which intensified concerns over influences of nihilistic violence extremism (NVE) online.
The ban on Discord, however, sparked criticisms from users who use the platforms for jobs, businesses, and other non-gaming related purposes.
On Thursday, September 24, the CICC publicly apologized to the inconvenienced users, admitting that they were unaware that Discord is not exclusively a game-messaging platform.

articles.title: Africa's richest man helps fund $660m fuel pipeline between Ethiopia and Djibouti
articles.summary: The pipeline would strengthen energy security in landlocked Ethiopia, while creating jobs at Djibouti's port.

blocks.text: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote, Ethiopia and Djibouti have agreed to develop a $660m (£500m) petroleum pipeline and storage project linking the two countries.
The project will include a 120km- (75 mile-) pipeline connecting Djibouti's Damerjog port to a distribution facility in Dewele, Ethiopia, as well as storage capacity of about 400 million litres.
It is expected to begin operations within 18 months.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said the pipeline would reduce the time needed to transport fuel from Djibouti's port to the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, from five days to one.
The first phase will transport key petroleum products, including jet fuel, diesel and petrol.
Speaking at the groundbreaking ceremony, Dangote said the project would strengthen Ethiopia's energy security and make its fuel supply chain more resilient.

Landlocked Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti's port for imports, including petroleum products. The new infrastructure is expected to reduce pressure on existing transport systems supporting industries, including transport, aviation, agriculture and construction.
Djibouti is also expected to benefit from increased port activity, job creation and higher government revenues.
The project is part of Dangote's wider expansion of infrastructure and manufacturing businesses across Africa.

Dangote Cement has production capacity of about 55 million tonnes a year, while his oil refinery in Nigeria currently has capacity to process 700,000 barrels of crude a day and is seeking to double that to 1.4 million barrels a day.
The refinery recently listed 4.1 billion ordinary shares on the Nigerian stock exchange, aiming to raise about $1.63bn (£1.2bn).
In Kenya, the company is due to break ground next week on a proposed 700,000-barrel-a-day crude oil refinery in Lamu.

articles.title: ‘She never accepted no’: Liam Neeson on dogged heroine behind Tuam mass baby grave film
articles.summary:
Catherine Corless’s exposure of almost 800 infant deaths at a home led by nuns prompted Neeson to bring the story to screen

Liam…

blocks.text: Liam Neeson still remembers his shock and shame when he read a New York Times article about the mother and baby institution in Tuam, County Galway.

It was 2017 and the article chronicled the campaign by Catherine Corless, an amateur local historian, to expose abuse and neglect by Irish nuns that led to hundreds of children being buried in a mass, unmarked grave.

“I had such a visceral reaction,” Neeson told the Guardian. “I’m obviously Irish, I was raised in the Catholic church, and I had a deep sense of embarrassment and obligation for the truth to come out and for there to be some accountability.”

blocks.caption: Liam Neeson, the producer of The Lost Children of Tuam, says he felt a deep sense of obligation to expose the truth. Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty for IMDb

blocks.text: It prompted the actor – and former altar boy – to use his heft in the film industry to become a producer for the first time. He optioned the article, visited Corless at her home and assembled a team to put the story on screen.

The result, nine years later, is The Lost Children of Tuam, a feature film that is released in Ireland this week and in the UK next month. “This was such an important story for the world to know about and to give a voice to the hundreds of babies and children that died,” said Neeson.

The release coincides with the continuing excavation of a 5,000 sq metre (53,820 sq ft) site where the Bon Secours order is believed have interred 796 infants who died at the St Mary’s mother and baby home between 1925 and 1961.

blocks.caption: Catherine Corless at the site of the former mother and baby home in Tuam, County Galway, where it is believed 796 infants were buried. Photograph: Rory Carroll/The Guardian

blocks.text: An international team of forensic archaeologists and other specialists has found skeletal remains of 99 babies and children since starting work last year – the result of Corless’s research, a judicial commission and a promise by the Irish state to seek truth and justice for survivors and relatives of those who died.

It is part of a wider reckoning of the mistreatment of women and children in state- and religious-run institutions across Ireland. Tuam, however, stands out for its macabre details – some infants were buried in a disused subterranean septic tank – and the doggedness of the woman who exposed it.

blocks.caption: Monica Dolan, who plays Catherine Corless, in a scene from The Lost Children of Tuam. Photograph: Element Pictures

blocks.text: In her quest for answers, Corless never accepted “no”, said Neeson. “The detective work she did to uncover this atrocity involving the relationship between the state and the church was extraordinary.”

The film, based on the New York Times article by Dan Barry, tells the story of how Corless, a former textile factory secretary with an interest in local history, began researching the site for an essay. Officials and the Bon Secours order fobbed her off but Corless discovered that 796 children had died without burial records before the institution was closed in 1961 and demolished.

Early reviews of the film, which was written by Rebecca Lenkiewicz and directed by Frank Berry, say it is sensitive and stirring, with the English actor Monica Dolan giving a powerful central performance.

blocks.caption: Director Frank Berry, Monica Dolan and Liam Neeson promote The Lost Children of Tuam in Toronto. Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty for IMDb

blocks.text: “She’s brilliant – so natural, so down to earth,” said Corless. “She portrayed me as I am. She has an English accent so how on earth did she capture the way I speak?”
Andrew Bennett, who plays her husband, Aidan, has also captured his personality and the couple’s relationship, she said.

Corless has watched the film three times – two private viewings for her family and survivors, and the premiere at the Galway film Fleadh in July, where it won best Irish film. “I was so nervous I needed to see it a few times,” she said.

blocks.caption: Andrew Bennett and Monica Dolan, who play Aidan and Catherine Corless. The actors have captured their personality and relationship, says Corless. Photograph: Element Pictures

blocks.text: “We’re ordinary people. We have a farm. That a film would be made about us, it was out of this world. It’s done with great respect, with the odd little bit of humour in it too, and it just hits people, it hits you hard.”

Berry, the director, said the film showed Corless’s integrity and persistence. “Her work revealed a lot of very hard truths about Ireland. It’s a way of telling truths but with an inspirational central character. It shows that one person can achieve amazing things.”

articles.title: US and China must act as responsible powers together, Xi says as Trump toasts friendship at state dinner
articles.summary: Trump said he and Xi had "never gotten along better" as he hosted the Chinese president at the lavish White House event.
articles.byline: Bernd Debusmann, Max Matza, Ione Wells

blocks.text: Trump thanked Xi for making the long trip to the US, and said the relationship between the two men was strong.
"We've never gotten along better," Trump said.
He praised the long history of US-China relations, although he did take an unscripted detour to praise his ongoing ballroom project.
In the off-the-cuff moment, he said as a "special treat" the Chinese leader and his wife could be the first to enter the ballroom, which is still a year away from completion.
"Anybody who wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and clean and sparkling, it's our honour to have you do so," he said.
He also presented Xi with a sculpture of a bald eagle, America's national symbol, saying it embodied "the free and soaring spirit of America".
"We hope it will find a nice, wonderful place in Beijing. It's your honour," he said.
Trump added that he and First Lady Melania had participated in the design of the sculpture.
Xi thanked his hosts for receiving him and his wife with "meticulous care and consideration", making them "feel truly at home".
He said the two leaders are "making history in our bilateral engagements".

"We agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability," Xi said, adding that the two shared "sincere and in-depth exchanges" that will strengthen relations between the two countries.
Like Trump's, Xi's remarks were heavy on flattery, focusing on cultural ties and shared history between the US and China.

The relationship between the two countries was "forged in blood and fire" during the fight against Japan in the Second World War, before being furthered during the "ping pong" diplomacy of the Nixon administration, he said.
Towards the end of his speech, Xi said the US and China's goals can be "mutually reinforcing". He urged both sides to explore a "new approach for major countries to get along".

When the BBC entered the dining hall for the dinner, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was standing over a table and appeared to be telling an entertaining story that had two others nearby barreled over with laughter.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was at another table, with a serious look on his face. His wife is sat beside him, with Jared Kushner and White House chief of staff Monica Crowley nearby.
The White House invited scores of US officials, as well as conservative broadcasters, tech industry bosses, social media CEOs and other corporate executives.
Attendees included members of Trump's cabinet, as well as family members like his children Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany.
Bosses from the tech industry in attendance included Apple's Tim Cook, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google's Sundar Pichai, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Both Cook and Huang were seated at the same table as Trump and Xi. As was Musk, who previously worked in Trump's administration leading the effort to shrink government.
Other companies whose leaders were in attendance include General Motors, Visa, Paramount Skydance, ExxonMobil and more.
Social media mogul Mark Zuckerberg also attended, as well as Jeff Yaas, the American billionaire who owns a share of TikTok.
"Everybody wanted to be there," Trump said ahead of the event. "I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world, and a lot more."
But one notable absence was Anthropic - one of the biggest and most valuable AI firms in the world. The BBC has asked Anthropic if it was invited, or if they chose not to be there.

articles.title: ‘Wake-up call’: Labor considers changing Australian laws after OpenAI Medicare hack
articles.summary:
Expert says Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a crime

The federal government could change Australian…

blocks.text: The federal government could change Australian laws if the current legal framework could not respond to the unprecedented OpenAI hack of Medicare, ministers have confirmed.

On Friday, the government said the review by spy agency, the Australian signals directorate, would consider whether legislative change was needed after the prime minister revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare’s statistics website and three other systems in June.
If current laws could not touch the tech giant, they would need updating, environment minister Murray Watt said on Friday.

“There’s now a review of this underway through that task force that we’ve appointed, and one of the things that they’ll be looking at is whether these matters can be referred to the Australian federal police under current Australian law,” he told Channel Seven’s Sunrise program.
“If that is possible to happen, then that will happen. If it’s not possible, then clearly that indicates that we need to change Australian laws, and that’s what we’ll be doing.”

The assistant minister for technology and the digital economy, Andrew Charlton, acknowledged similar incidents would become “more and more prevalent into the future” and the government would need to be prepared.

“That’s why we’re conducting a review of the incident as well as a review of the laws to determine exactly … whether there needs to be legislative change to recognise this type of incident conducted by an AI agent rather than directly by a person or a company,” Charlton told ABC radio.
Labor has announced it would legislate an AI standard, which Charlton said would be informed by the rapid review. The government has said it wants the bill to be introduced by the end of the year.

UNSW professor Lyria Bennett Moses, an academic expert in technology and law, said Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault, such as intention or knowledge, is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a crime.
She said existing laws are clear if a human or corporation gains unauthorised access to restricted data, but it’s more complicated when an AI agent commits the physical element of the offence.
“The person is not the AI agent, so it’s not about what the AI agent intended. It’s about how you attribute that intention and that knowledge back to a corporation,” Bennett Moses said.

Bennett Moses said existing civil laws are more likely to deal with these sorts of incidents, that would allow a government or individual to seek compensation an AI company for harm “negligently caused by that corporation”.

“If their systems have suffered harm and there is financial loss, and that harm was caused by the negligence of a corporation, you’ve got a potential for litigation to get compensation for that harm,” she said.
“Here it seems to me much easier to hold a company liable, because if a company caused the harm, it’s not a defence to say that my bot did it.”
Anthony Albanese told the Asia Society on Thursday that the incident was a “wake-up call” about the risks of AI, and whether humans would remain in charge of the technology.
“This technology is moving very, very fast, and we need to make sure that we have a responsibility to keep on top of it,” Albanese said.
On Friday, the prime minister addressed the United Nations and called on other countries to act to “shape artificial intelligence development, rather than be passively shaped by it”.
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told reporters the opposition would be open to working with the government to hold companies accountable.

“I’ve long believed that data breaches need to be dealt with in an appropriate way and those responsible for the data breaches need to be accountable for it … But we’ll wait and see what the government has in mind.”

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said on Thursday the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”.

“During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement.
Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”.

articles.title: Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change
articles.summary: Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah called the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods a "warning to the world" — and questioned if the world had "really heard that warning."

image.caption: Residents carry their belongings salvaged from their damaged homes filled with mud and debris [File: August 29, 2026 ] Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Four weeks after catastrophic flash floods ravaged Nepal, the small Himalayan country's prime minister stood at the podium of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) to warn leaders about the impact of a warming world.

"I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions," Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in his UNGA address Thursday.
Nepal's leader calls for cooperation to protect the Himalayas
The Nepalese leader stressed that the perils of climate change transcend national borders as he made a case for greater international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas.

"The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system," Shah said, proposing the establishment of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, which he said would be led by Nepal, India and China.

Shah elaborated that the mechanism would help countries share satellite data and expertise, as well as monitor glacial lakes that pose a threat. He also called for stronger joint early-warning systems and coordinated, cross-border assistance in the event of a disaster.
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information," the prime minister said.

blocks.caption: Nepal's prime minister was the youngest head of government to address the UN General AssemblyImage: Ryan Murphy/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: Nepal paying 'colossal' price for climate change
Shah noted that his country contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
"We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," he said, adding that he was not blaming any individual nation or continent.
"We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity," Shah said.
Grants, not loans, necessary for flood recovery
The Nepalese prime minister emphasized the principles of responsibility, reparation and resilience as he called for grant-based support rather than loans.
Shah said vulnerable nations should not be forced to take on additional debt to recover from climate catastrophes.

"When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants. We need adequate grant-based support from the world," he said.
The 36-year-old Shah was the youngest head of government to speak at the 81st session of the UNGA.
Nepal-Tibet floods — the deadly 'Himalayan tsunami'
On August 26, a glacier collapsed near the border between Nepal and China's ​Tibet Autonomous Region, unleashing landslides and a flash flood that ripped through downstream valleys.
In the days after the disaster, the world watched powerful images of the widespread destruction emerge from Nepal.
Entire villages were flattened. In other visuals, people trapped in hydropower tunnels deep within the Himalayas were seen crawling away a thick sludge of mud to reach rescuers.
Over 6,000 people are still reported to be missing, with search and recovery efforts still ongoing.

articles.title: Trillanes sought as witness on Duterte wealth allegations
articles.summary: They want him questioned over alleged P181.6-M transactions involving Sara Duterte and her family.

blocks.text: September 25, 2026 | 12:19pm
Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV files another plunder complaint against former President Rodrigo Duterte and Sen. Bong Go at the Department of Justice on Aug. 7, 2024.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui

MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial has asked the Senate impeachment court to subpoena former Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV to testify on allegations involving her unexplained wealth next week.
In a manifestation before the impeachment court released on Thursday, September 24, the prosecution sought Trillanes' testimony in connection with Article II of the Articles of Impeachment.

Article II covers allegations involving Duterte's unexplained wealth and her alleged receipt or acquisition of funds from persons or sources identified in evidence presented before the impeachment court.
The prosecution's request comes as it presents evidence on Duterte's alleged unexplained wealth, including allegations previously raised by Trillanes.
P181.6 million alleged funds
Trillanes earlier testified before the House Committee on Justice during its impeachment proceedings against Duterte.

In April, he alleged that five members of the Duterte family, including Sara Duterte and her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, received or encashed P181.6 million in checks allegedly from Davao drug lord Samuel "Sammy" Uy between 2011 and 2013.

The former senator made the allegation in a sworn affidavit presented during the House impeachment hearing on April 22. The House panel was also shown bank transaction records that Trillanes said supported his claim.
According to Trillanes, Sara Duterte received P22.3 million in three transactions, while Rodrigo Duterte was listed at P15.6 million.
Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte was listed at P51.5 million, while former Davao City mayor and now Rep. Paolo Duterte was listed at P38.8 million.
Honeylet Avanceña, Rodrigo Duterte's common-law partner, and her daughter Veronica Duterte were listed at P53.2 million combined, according to Trillanes.
Trillanes said the transactions followed a similar pattern, with checks issued at regular intervals over about two years, often in identical or near-identical amounts.
Other witnesses
The prosecution said Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System division chief Rendell Sopeña is expected to return to the witness stand on Monday.
Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte, the younger brother of Vice President Sara Duterte, has also been subpoenaed and could be presented as a witness on Monday or Tuesday.
Baste's testimony is expected to focus on the Davao City government's transactions with GenCorp Industries Inc., which secured 19 contracts with the city worth more than P33.2 million.
The vice president declared GenCorp as one of her business interests in her 2024 and 2025 SALNs.

Baste earlier said he and other Davao City officials were unaware of his sister's interest in GenCorp. He also said neither Sara Duterte's name nor the surname "Duterte" appeared in the company's official documents submitted for its transactions with the city.

The impeachment trial will continue to hear evidence under Article II, which covers allegations involving Duterte's wealth, SALN disclosures and alleged continued business interests while in office. — with a report from Cristina Chi

articles.title: Xi got Trump's red carpet welcome - but not everything he wanted
articles.summary: China wanted progress on trade, technology and Taiwan - but hasn't got as much as it would have hoped for.

blocks.text: Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go?
ByLaura Bicker
China correspondent
President Xi Jinping's summits with Donald Trump have one clear aim.
China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan.
On this visit, however, despite Trump rolling out the red carpet for him, the Chinese leader didn't get everything he wanted.
The trade truce that saw both countries pause a tit-for-tat tariff war and prevent a further escalation, was extended by only a few months - from November to January.
Beijing had hoped for at least a year as Xi looks to ride out the remainder of Trump's presidency.
This means key disputes on tariffs, China's dominance on rare earth supplies and access to advanced US chips are being kicked forward into yet another round of negotiations.
This suggests the US wants China to do more to fulfil its side of the bargain before offering longer-term concessions.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trump and Xi attend a dinner at the White House

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Trump and Xi attend a dinner at the White House

The uncomfortable truth for Xi is that his domestic economy is in trouble. While the country sells a record number of goods around the world, consumers at home are holding back. Youth unemployment remains stubbornly high and property prices have slumped in a country where 80% of people own their own homes.
Trade is helping to prop up growth, making access to overseas markets more important than ever. Xi needs to protect those exports from the kind of debilitating tariffs the US imposed last year.
On Taiwan, Xi once again made clear that US arms sales to Taiwan are a red line for China.
The US is bound by law to provide the self-governing island with the means to defend itself.
In May, Xi warned Trump that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict".
Trump then delayed the approval of a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, describing it as a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing.
Xi may have seized on that opening during the talks and likely argued that restraining support for Taiwan reduces the risk of conflict.
On Thursday he reiterated his hope that the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence.
However, Trump - who is coming under some bipartisan pressure to continue US support to Taiwan - is yet to make any public response to the Chinese leader's comments.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trade is helping to prop up growth

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Trade is helping to prop up growth
The two leaders did at least discuss artificial intelligence (AI) although it's unclear whether they agreed to any safeguards.

All eyes were on whether they would make any concrete decisions on AI - such as an agreement to hold a summit - in the wake of an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for the slowing down of AI development to make it safer. That followed a warning by a top safety researcher from the company that there was a "greater than 10% chance" that AI could cause the extinction of humans.

But besides Xi talking about the importance of ensuring AI "is always under human control" we didn't get much else. Trump has most recently dismissed fears of human extinction from the technology as a "hoax".

And, of course, let's not forget the pandas. The gift of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to Atlanta was first heralded in April, but Xi has now announced they will arrive in just a few days as China's panda diplomacy resumes.
There may be more announcements to come as the two prepare to have tea and visit the national archives on Friday.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pandas have played an important role in Chinese diplomatic measures

blocks.text: Pandas have played an important role in Chinese diplomatic measures
But for now, one of the summit's biggest victories for Beijing may have been the optics.

The lavish welcome, a personal greeting at the airport and a state banquet featuring sesame crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy have been welcomed by those watching from China. It will have helped cement Xi's image at home as Trump's equal.
Memes contrasting the two leaders have spread widely on Chinese social media. One popular image shows Trump grimacing as bomber jets fly overhead, while Xi remained impassive.

Xi has found a way to manage one of the world's most unpredictable leaders. But while Trump talks of a "truly great friendship", China's leader is focussed on something bigger: securing China's place alongside the United States as a superpower.
The pandas, the pageantry and the warm words may help smooth this relationship. But beneath the spectacle, the competition between the world's two most powerful countries remains as fierce as ever.

articles.title: Marcos signs law postponing 2026 barangay, SK elections
