articles.title: Jürgen Klopp starts Germany job with shaky Netherlands draw
articles.summary: A late Netherlands goal denied Jürgen Klopp a win in his first match as Germany coach. The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund boss has big ambitions, but the game showed he's going to need more…

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp's first Germany game ended in a Nations League drawImage: Malte Ossowski/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: It looked, until the final moments, as though Germany would somehow hold on and grant Jürgen Klopp a victory in his first game as Germany coach.

"It felt mostly good," Klopp told German broadcaster RTL after the match, with his voice strained after a typically energetic display on the sidelines. "That was really exhausting for both teams today." He added that he naturally wanted a win but that he can "live with the point, too."

In the end, an injury time Cody Gakpo goal meant Klopp and his team had to settle for a 1-1 draw in their Nations League opener against the Netherlands. While the timing of the equalizer will sting, Germany was second best for much of the contest, which turned a ill-tempered at times. Nevertheless, Klopp was upbeat.
"I was very, very, very satisfied with many of the individual performances," he said, before admitting that "we can play better football and create more chances — that's for sure."

Gakpo plays his club football for Liverpool, where Klopp coached for more than eight years. So too does Dutch captain Virgil van Dijk, who thought he'd opened the scoring for the hosts early on, only to see his headed goal ruled out. A close-range finish from Lukas Nmecha then gave Germany the lead but not control of the game.
New faces, new coach, not yet new Germany

While there were a few patches of attacking play that resembled the kind of high-intensity, exhilarating football that Klopp produced at Liverpool and, before that, at Borussia Dortmund, Germany looked shaky at the back and were thankful for some wasteful Dutch finishing.

It is, though, difficult to judge much at this early stage. Klopp replaced Julian Nagelsmann after another poor World Cup showing from Germany and, after naming two different squads for the four Nations Leagues games in an extended international period, is still assessing how to make the most of what he has. Three players — Younes Ebnoutalib, Yannik Engelhardt and Philipp Treu — made debuts on Thursday, and more are likely follow over the next three games.

"I won't promise anything [in terms of trophies]. What I can promise is that we will definitely give it a try," he told reporters ahead of the game. "There's an impression that we have less quality than other countries. When things aren't working, you take a closer look and try to bring about changes. That's what we're working on now."

After Germany lost Kai Havertz to injury in the first half, having already had to change to starting XI after Jamal Musiala pulled out of the match in the warmup, the team was left without much of their attacking experience and class.
Klopp's record should buy him time
But Klopp won't panic. His methods, both tactically and emotionally, will take time to bear fruit. At Liverpool, it took nearly five years to win a trophy; at Dortmund, it took three.

"When the system isn't yet in place and the processes aren't yet established, then something like this happens," he said about Wednesday's performance. "I was very pleased with the passion, the intensity, but we can definitely play better."

Usually, waiting for success would not be acceptable for German national team fans. But after repeated recent failures, and with Klopp a popular figure, he has more credit in that bank than his predecessor, Julian Nagelsmann. The last coach to win a World Cup for Germany, Joachim Löw, said he will need it.

blocks.caption: Jürgen Klopp has combined experienced internationals and newcomers in his first squadsImage: Christian Schulze/nordphoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: "It is crucial now to give him the necessary time and space to implement his ideas," he told the Münchner Merkur/tz newspaper. "Jürgen stands for energy, intensity and a strong bond between the team and the fans. But even for him, not everything will work from one day to the next. After a disappointing World Cup, it takes trust, patience and a team that once again plays for Germany with great conviction."
Klopp calls for German unity, seeks Greece win

Klopp has already tried to unite the country behind the team. On the touchline in Amsterdam, he ran through his familiar repertoire of fist bumps, beaming smiles and growls at officials in a cap emblazoned with the words "one of 83 million" on it.

The headgear has already become a familiar sight. It's a reference to Germany's population and the 59-year-old has also referenced the importance of his team, and their flag, as a symbol of nationhood at a time when the far-right AfD (Alternative for Germany) are making substantial electoral gains.

"I'd like to reclaim the flag for myself — or for us," Klopp said. "I want us to always wave it in a way that makes no one think: 'What's wrong with you?' But, rather, that people simply get the feeling that you're happy and understand how lucky you are to have been born, raised or moved to this wonderful country."

While Klopp's charisma makes such a lofty ambition seem somewhat feasible, he's also pragmatic enough to know that for the German national team to be universally loved, it needs to win. Augsburg on Saturday, against Greece in the Nations League, would be a good place to start.

articles.title: Netanyahu defends Israeli military actions in Middle East in UN speech
articles.summary: Dozens of delegates walked out in protest as he took the podium, with the Israeli leader labelling them "moral cowards".

blocks.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has fiercely defended his country's military campaigns in Iran, Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East in a speech to the UN General Assembly.
After dozens of delegates walked out in protest as he took to the stage, Netanyahu vowed to continue fighting: "We're going to win. We have no other choice."
In response to the walkout, he said: "If there are any other moral cowards who haven't left the hall, please do so now."
The Israeli leader also rejected accusations that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.

Hours earlier, in a recorded message Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas told the UN that Israeli policies - in particular the illegal expansion of Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank - threatened "the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland".
He also said it jeopardised the two-state solution, which is an internationally backed formula for peace between Israel and the Palestinians.
Abbas said that Palestinians were being subjected to "killing, destruction, starvation and attempts at displacement, as well as a genocidal war" in Gaza by the Israeli military.
The Palestinian leader was addressing the annual gathering via a video link because had been denied a US entry visa.
Netanyahu, who is subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes, launched scathing attacks on nations and leaders who have criticised him.
"They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism - some colonialism. And who's accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God's sake, they invented the term," he said.
He went on to label Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan a "tyrant", accusing him of supporting the Palestinian armed group Hamas.
Erdogan told the UN on Tuesday that the injustices faced by those in Gaza and the West Bank "deeply offends the conscience of humanity".
New York City's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani - who had previously vowed to arrest Netanyahu but later said he did not have the authority to do so - was also criticised by the Israeli leader.
"Since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York," the Israeli prime minister said.
In a statement, Mamdani's office said Netanyahu "used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians".
Netanyahu also thanked US President Donald Trump for his "bold leadership", referring to the air strikes the US and Israel jointly launched against Tehran in February.
"Israel and America acted together not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilisation," he said.
A number of people protesting against Netanyahu's visit were detained in New York City. Among them were the Oscar-winning actress Susan Sarandon and Emmy-winning actress Hannah Einbinder.
The Israeli military launched a ground offensive in the Gaza Strip after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack against Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostages.
During the Israeli military campaign more than 73,920 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.
Last year, the world's leading association of genocide scholars declared that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza.
A resolution passed by the International Association of Genocide Scholars (IAGS) stated that Israel's conduct meets the legal definition as laid out in the UN convention on genocide.
Israel has regularly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide and says they are justified as a means of self-defence.
On 28 February, Israel and the US started launching massive air strikes on Iran, suspecting it of secretly building a nuclear weapon - a claim denied by Tehran.
Iran retaliated by carrying out missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases.

articles.title: Australia news live: Paterson says PM’s AI hack timing not a coincidence; Gen Z going without for a house
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live.

  • Get our breaking news email, free…

blocks.text: Australia’s Gen Z are the generation most willing to cut their spending way back to afford a home, according to Cotality data reported by AAP.

The figures show more than 75% of all Australians were curbing their outgoings in pursuit of property, meaning we are more likely to do so than our Canadian, US and UK peers (for whom the figures sat below 70%).
Levels of discretionary spending, like eating out, owning a car, and even moving from the family home into a sharehouse, have dropped among young adults in recent years.

But it wasn’t just first-time buyers making significant financial sacrifices to climb the ladder. Millennials – the largest buyer cohort in the world – are readily forgoing small luxuries to afford homes large enough for their families.
Prospective buyers were selling their second car or putting off holidays while their children were young, Capital Buyers Agency owner Claire Corby said.
double quotation markFor many, it’s around delaying things like going away, or reducing things like dinners out. People are leaving where they want to live and buying in cheaper markets.
Most Australians would not be persuaded to participate in the housing market until mortgage interest rates hit a 4.9% average, the data revealed.
The average rate for an owner-occupier in August 2026 was 6.3%, meaning the market is likely to stay quiet for some time and allowing bold buyers to swoop in.
double quotation markPeople are being conservative and cautious.

blocks.caption: Catie McLeod

blocks.text: Catie McLeod
The opposition’s defence spokesperson, James Paterson, has questioned the timing of the prime minister’s announcement that an AI agent hacked Medicare.

Paterson made the claim on the ABC’s 7.30 program last night after Anthony Albanese publicly disclosed that an AI agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and that the tech giant only notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a “public mailbox”.
Paterson told 7.30 he believed Albanese had chosen to make the announcement at the UN summit in New York, as part of his effort to stand up to “big tech” on AI.
The senator said:

double quotation markThe government has questions to answer about when they knew and … why the prime minister decided to disclose it in the way he did in the place he did at the time he did. But in terms of the nature of the potential of actual security breach this is the bottom end of the spectrum of seriousness. I don’t think it was a coincidence. I think it neatly dove-tailed with the political agenda the prime minister has in New York City.

Paterson said he didn’t consider the breach to be overly serious because the data the AI agent accessed was made freely available to researchers and academics studying the health system, and was not personal or private in nature.
He said the breach was cause for “being alert but not alarmed”.
Nevertheless, he said Australians were “entitled to demand explanations and contrition” and to want high levels of confidence when entering into agreements with big tech companies such as OpenAI.
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Nick Visser with the main action.

articles.title: Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class
articles.summary: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate".

blocks.text: The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any one class.
A 30% cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate".
Opposition parties accuse the government of pandering to the policies of the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party, ahead of a general election next year.

Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the limit is "purely linguistic" rather than one of citizenship, while he has sought to frame the ban on the niqab and burqa as a matter of gender equality.
"You must go to school with your face uncovered," Meloni said while announcing the plans on Sunday, adding that no-one could decide that a young woman should hide herself in the name of tradition.
There were several drafts of the decree ahead of Thursday's council of ministers meeting, however the core details were clear.
The veil ban would apply to the burqa and niqab, but not the hijab, which leaves the face visible.
The niqab is a veil for the face that leaves the area around the eyes clear. However, it may be worn with a separate eye veil. It is worn with an accompanying headscarf.
The burka is a one-piece veil that covers the face and body. Often there is a mesh screen around the eyes to see through.
Non-Italian citizens make up 11.6% of pupils in Italy's schools, according to the research institution Fondazione ISMU.
The 30% limit on pupils who speak limited Italian will cover separate stages of education differently.
In primary schools, it would cover non-Italian citizens who have either not been born in Italy or who have not attended at least two years of nursery school.
In lower- and upper- secondary schools, it would cover pupils without Italian citizenship who have not successfully completed at least three years in the Italian school system.

Local school offices would be asked to spread pupils with little Italian language skills more evenly among nearby schools. Where that is not possible, exemptions would apply, with extra Italian teaching.
The aim was to avoid "ghetto classes", the education minister explained.

The draft also goes further on parents, according to the Ansa news agency. Schools would have to report to social services cases in which persistent language barriers among those with parental responsibility hinder a child's integration. Free Italian courses would be offered.
The measure is a decree law, meaning it can take effect immediately, but must be ratified by parliament within 60 days.

Italy already has guidance on Italian language at schools. A 2010 ministerial notice under then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini set a 30% limit "as a rule" on pupils without Italian citizenship. The new decree puts the limit into law.
The political opposition says the plan is as much about politics as schools.
Opponents accuse Meloni of pandering to Roberto Vannacci, a retired military general who leads the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party and is seen as a threat to the governing coalition's right flank.

The leader of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD), Elly Schlein, called the plan propaganda and impossible to implement. PD deputy and chamber vice-president Anna Ascani also accused the government of propaganda at the expense of schoolchildren.
Valditara, speaking by video link from New York at a press conference rejected the charge.
"We are not chasing Vannacci; if anything, he is chasing us," he said.
Vannacci said he agreed with the measures, but they should have come years ago.
The League's Matteo Salvini, who launched a separate package of measures on what he called "political Islam" on Wednesday, accused Vannacci of "continually voting against the government".
Salvini said he hoped Futuro Nazionale would back the League's new proposals.

articles.title: Priest killed and four injured in knife attack at Polish abbey
articles.summary: A male suspect from Ukraine was arrested after the stabbings in the town of Jarosław, police say.

blocks.text: A priest has been killed and four other people injured in a knife attack in south-east Poland, officials have said.
A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arrested after the stabbings on the grounds of a Catholic abbey in the town of Jarosław.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki said Thursday's attack "has shaken us all and demands a firm response from the state", while his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky said "we are shocked by this evil".

Reports in Polish media said the attacker first injured a priest in a nearby cafe, and then another four people inside the abbey itself. A police investigation into the attacker's motives is now under way.
Polish police said four men and one woman were stabbed in the attack on Thursday morning on the abbey grounds.
The name of the murdered priest has not been publicly released.
Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said psychological support was now being provided to all those affected by the incident.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the perpetrator "will be punished with the full severity of Polish law".

Echoing his words, President Zelensky said "the perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility according to the law", adding that Ukraine was counting on "a quick and thorough investigation of all circumstances".
The Ukrainian embassy in Poland also condemned the attack.

In a statement, it said: "In such difficult moments, it is especially important to support each other, remain steadfast in respect for human life, and not allow pain to escalate into hatred or new violence. Responsibility for a crime must be based solely on the law."
Poland has recently seen a number of often violent incidents involving its citizens and Ukrainians, many of whom have fled their home country after Russia's full-scale invasion.

articles.title: Ed Miliband meets Iran’s foreign minister as Tehran gives US ultimatum on strait of Hormuz
articles.summary:
Senior Iranian officials say Washington has four to five days to respond to its conditions for reopening the strait

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has met his Iranian counterpart,…

blocks.text: The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has met his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, for the first time in New York amid warnings from senior Iranian security officials that the US has four to five days to respond to its conditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz.

The previously unknown apparent deadline was specified by Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the supreme national security council, in a TV interview on Wednesday evening, and it is unclear what action Tehran will take if the US does not respond to Iran’s preconditions for reopening the vital waterway.

A faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday.

Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond.

Rezaei, a recently promoted hardliner, said Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and Araghchi had flown to New York to convey Iran’s internally agreed terms, not to negotiate new ones. “There has been no discussion whatsoever that these conditions should change, that a new condition should be removed or added,” he said.
The big change appears to be that Tehran now insists Washington act first. “Talk is enough. Negotiations are enough. Now we must act,” Rezaei said.
He warned that if the US did “not fulfil the conditions, we will neither open the strait of Hormuz nor is there any negotiation on the table”.

blocks.caption: The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi (left), speaks with his Jordanian counterpart, Ayman Safadi, at the UN in New York. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Rezaei said the seven conditions must be implemented “completely and all at once”, adding that the US had been given “four or five days” to do so. After that, he said, Iran would determine its “next step”, without specifying what that would entail.

The meeting between Miliband and Araghchi, one of an exhaustive round of bilaterals undertaken by the Iranian foreign minister, is the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers for a year and the first exchange since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries.
Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen.

He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to the British couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment in Tehran.
Overall, European diplomats have not sensed a US-Iran breakthrough in New York.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, also said it would be wrong to characterise the Witkoff talks with Iran as a major breakthrough. It is understood that Araghchi, speaking largely through a Qatari mediator, set out to him the seven preconditions to be met before it is willing to reopen the strait, including the lifting of US sanctions and an end to war on all fronts, a reference to Israeli military activity in south Lebanon.

Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis.

Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: “If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.”

Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to “the US bully” with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks.
He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases.

Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: “We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from the United Nations podium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.”

articles.title: UNGA Day 4: Lebanese on deck after defiant Netanyahu speech
articles.summary: A day after a divisive speech by Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu, the prime minister of Lebanon will address the UN General Assembly. Leaders from Pakistan and Iraq are also set to speak on the…
articles.byline: Wesley Dockery, Mark Hallam, Felix Tamsut, Jon Shelton

image.caption: Netanyahu spoke to a sparsely-populated chamber after a mass walkoutImage: Heather Khalifa/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 25, 2026
Welcome back to our coverage
We are resuming our coverage of the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, September 25.
The general debate is scheduled to begin its fourth day of the assembly at 9 a.m. New York time (1300 UTC).
Iraq, Pakistan, Lebanon and others are to speak in today's morning session, while countries such as Egypt, Mexico, Kazakhstan and Sweden will take the stand in the afternoon.
Friday's debate comes after a day of speeches that was centered on Gaza, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's address sparking a walkout by several delegates.

articles.title: Four civilians killed in Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan, Taliban says
articles.summary: Pakistan says it struck 10 targets, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives".

blocks.text: Afghanistan's Taliban government said a wave of Pakistani air strikes had killed four civilians in the latest escalation between the two sides.

The strikes hit provinces including Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, sources told the BBC. A resident told AFP news agency they heard a jet, followed by a large explosion and then a fire in the city.
Pakistan said its forces had struck 10 targets in Afghanistan, without specifying their locations, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives".
It's the second wave of Pakistani air strikes on Afghan territory in the past week, and comes after a deadly attack on a police facility in Pakistan on 18 September.
In a statement, the Taliban said there would be an "appropriate response" following the attack, while Pakistan said any further "provocative act" would be responded to.
Taliban government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said the attacks were in Afghanistan's Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces.
In Paktia, an official said jets had bombed the Afghan Armed Forces' 203 Mansouri Corps, which is controlled by the Taliban, without providing any information on casualties.
In Khost, a spokesman said houses were damaged in the strikes, with no casualties reported. Abdullah, a local eyewitness, told Reuters news agency the strikes happened around midnight.
"People were shouting, and there was panic all around," he said. "Afterwards, the village elder arrived and called out to the houses, asking if anyone was killed. Thankfully, no one was killed."
Another local, Salamat Khan, told Reuters that "there is no military base here, nor are there any military personnel", adding "there are only the homes of ordinary civilians".
Zabihullah Mujahid labelled the attack as "reckless, careless, and hostile", and said it "will have adverse consequences for the Pakistani military".

Pakistan's Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the strikes were "deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan".

The Taliban and Pakistan had enjoyed three months of relative calm, until fighting reignited following an attack on a mosque at a police compound in north-western Pakistan last week, which killed at least 31 people, according to AFP.
A group linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has waged a violent campaign against Pakistan for years, claimed the attack.
Islamabad has accused Kabul of harbouring the TTP. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies this, saying militancy is Pakistan's internal problem.
Following the attack on the police facility, Pakistan said earlier this week it launched air strikes in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants.

Farid Dehqan, a spokesman for the Taliban government in Kunar province, told the BBC that three people were killed and four others were injured in the strike. The UN mission Unama also confirmed that at least three civilians were killed.

Then on Wednesday, Pakistan said it detected drones launched from Afghanistan into its territory and that all of them were "neutralised". Taliban officials denied that their government had launched drones against Pakistan that day.

Unama said in July that cross-border armed violence between Taliban government forces and Pakistani security forces killed at least 499 civilians and wounded 1,216 others between October 2025 and June 2026.

The worst single incident occurred in March, when more than 269 people were killed, external in a Pakistani air strike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation centre. Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure".
The neighbouring countries had agreed a ceasefire in March, but international mediation has failed to produce a lasting resolution.

During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly earlier this week, Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called for "concrete and verifiable" measures to ensure that Afghan territory is not used for "terrorism".

articles.title: Three-way battle for power in world chess: Who will be elected FIDE president in Samarkand?
articles.summary: The era of Russian presidents is coming to an end at the World Chess Federation (FIDE). Two Germans and one Kazakh are up for election. Among the issues at play are money, Kremlin influence, and…

image.caption: FIDE presidential candidate Wadim Rosenstein is also an avid playerImage: Meurer/Beautiful Sports/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Gens una sumus" ("We are one family") is the motto of the World Chess Federation (FIDE). Yet when officials from some 200 countries gather for their congress in Samarkand on Saturday, September 26, it is not likely to feel like a joyous family reunion.

A new FIDE president is to be elected in Uzbekistan, and a three-way, politically charged race for the post has erupted, with the outcome uncertain. It has been clear since July that the incumbent FIDE president, Arkady Dvorkovich, would not be standing for re-election. The European Union had placed the former Russian deputy prime minister on its sanctions list due to his support for Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine.
Three entrepreneurs vying for the top job

The candidates standing for election are Kazakh billionaire Timur Turlov and two Germans: investor Jan Henric Buettner and entrepreneur Wadim Rosenstein, who is running as the official candidate of the German Chess Federation (DSB).

For the first time in over 30 years, FIDE will not be led by a Russian. Nevertheless, the three contenders repeatedly face two questions: What are their ties to Russia? And where do the millions come from that FIDE uses to finance itself and its competitions? For the Kremlin, chess remains a component of Russia's soft power, and little happens within FIDE without financial backers linked to Russia.
Jan Henric Buettner: The Formula 1 model

Buettner is arguably the best positioned to answer these questions. A native of Hamburg, he has made a name for himself in the chess world through his collaboration with former world champion Magnus Carlsen. The 62-year-old German has no known ties to Moscow that would require explanation. On the contrary: "We are the only team with no connection to Russia," Malcolm Pein — Buettner's candidate for vice president — told DW.

blocks.caption: Jan Henric Buettner (3rd from left) is championing "Freestyle" chess alongside former world champion Magnus Carlsen (2nd from left).Image: Gregor Fischer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Buettner and his running mate say they intend to reduce reliance on Russian financial backers and make chess commercially successful. Buettner plans to distribute 20% of FIDE's revenue to chess federations worldwide. The former AOL executive looks to Formula 1 motor racing as his model – a vision likely considered too radical by many officials in the chess world. Consequently, Buettner is seen as having only an outside chance of winning.
Timur Turlov: The establishment candidate

The favorite to become FIDE's new president is Timur Turlov. Born in Moscow, he became a Kazakh citizen in 2022 and is one of the wealthiest men in the Central Asian nation. The entrepreneur is considered a close associate of outgoing President Dvorkovich and, by extension, a member of the FIDE establishment. Regarding finances, too, the status quo is likely to remain unchanged under the 38-year-old; after all, Turlov's publicly traded financial firm, Freedom Holding Corp., has been FIDE's main sponsor for many years.

The prospect of Turlov potentially holding the dual roles of FIDE president and major financial backer does not sit well with everyone in the chess community. Furthermore, Freedom Holding Corp. and its CEO are currently on Ukraine's sanctions list. Ukrainian authorities accuse Turlov's company of helping to finance Russia's war of aggression. Press reports also suggest that the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has taken an interest in Turlov's financial firm.
Report: Hamburger Sparkasse closes account

In the spring of 2026, Turlov acquired the Hamburg-based chess software company Chessbase. Shortly thereafter, the German chess news website perlenvombodensee.de reported that the company's principal bank, Hamburger Sparkasse, had closed the Chessbase business account.

blocks.caption: Timur Turlov of Kazakhstan is considered the favorite in the race for the FIDE presidencyImage: Sergei Fadeichev/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chessbase declined to comment on the matter. Hamburger Sparkasse also did not address the specific case but told DW: "If a business relationship falls under currently existing sanctions – for example, against countries such as Russia, Belarus, or Iran – this may unfortunately result in us being unable to continue specific business relationships."
DW approached Timur Turlov for comment but had received no response by time of publication.
The position of Volodymyr Kovalchuk, vice president of the Ukrainian Chess Federation is clear.
"If Turlov wins the FIDE election and poses a threat to Ukraine's security, then we will push for him to be sanctioned by the EU as well," Kovalchuk told DW.
However, there are now signs of a rapprochement between Turlov and the Ukrainians: Turlov is currently advocating for a Ukrainian official to be elected as a vice president on the FIDE board.
Wadim Rosenstein: Many outstanding questions
The third figure in the mix, Wadim Rosenstein, is also facing intense scrutiny in Ukraine.
"It is absolutely clear that we will not support such a candidate and, should he be elected, will also propose him for sanctions," Kovalchuk said.
Rosenstein was born in 1990 in what is now Ukraine and moved to Germany at the age of nine. In the autumn of 2022, the entrepreneur and amateur chess player began organizing elaborate chess events.

Questions have dogged him ever since, with his business activities and connections to Russia being the primary focus of this scrutiny. According to Rosenstein, the companies within his Düsseldorf-based "WR Group" operate in various sectors, ranging from toilet paper trading and real estate to industrial logistics. Until 2022, a key focus was supporting German companies in regions including Ukraine and Russia, Rosenstein told DW a few months ago. However, he said he was no longer active in Russia; instead positioning himself "globally" across "70 countries," including Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkey.

blocks.caption: DSB President Paul Meyer-Dunker supports Wadim Rosenstein's bid to become the next FIDE presidentImage: Sebastian Kahnert/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The company in Russia
However, one of the Düsseldorf entrepreneur's remaining companies in Russia has enjoyed economic success in recent years. In July, Rosenstein told DW that these companies were active "only on paper."

It has since become clear that "WR RUS," at least, is anything but a paper tiger. The Moscow-based company has been owned by Rosenstein since 2021. Publicly available data show that "WR RUS's" profit grew from around €300,000 ($341,230) to €1.7 million ($1.93 million) between 2022 and 2025.

Furthermore, records confirm that Rosenstein's German companies – "WR Logistics" and "WR Certification" – collaborated with "WR RUS" through the end of 2023. Documents from "WR RUS" also show a dividend payment equivalent to around €30,000 for the year 2023, which apparently went to him and one of his German companies.
DW again approached Wadim Rosenstein for comment on these matters but received no response by the time of publication of this report.
High-priced players, upscale venues

Since 2022, millions have been poured into Rosenstein's elaborate chess events year after year. The list of Rosenstein's events is long: it includes a top-tier tournament featuring world number one Magnus Carlsen, the 2023 World Team Blitz and Rapid Chess Championship at the prestigious Rheinterrasse in Düsseldorf, and, most recently, the global "WR Women's Chess Tour." A premium venue in Stuttgart has been selected for the tour's finale in November – a location whose name the sponsor is likely to appreciate, Rosenstein Palace.

blocks.caption: A grand setting for the WR Women’s Chess Tour 2026: Rosenstein Palace in Stuttgart.Image: Markus Mainka/picture alliance

blocks.text: The FIDE presidential campaign is also costly. On social media, Rosenstein presents himself aboard a private jet during an international campaign tour. According to the Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper, a portion of the campaign costs is to be covered by Rosenstein's running mate for the vice-presidency – a wealthy real estate entrepreneur from Singapore.

Rosenstein has not disclosed the total cost of his numerous chess activities to date or the exact source of the funds. His company, "WR Logistics," is one of the main sponsors. Rosenstein told DW in July: "I have also used my own funds and brought on partners who trust me."
But who are these partners?
A sponsor that didn't exist

While Rosenstein was preparing his FIDE candidacy in April 2026, he introduced the Düsseldorf-based company "Glotech." He stated he was "proud to introduce our next partner." The sponsor is reportedly providing €250,000 for chess activities in Europe. According to Rosenstein, Glotech is "a true supporter of our vision."
However, according to Glotech Managing Director Evgeni Schukin, this support never existed: "There was no agreement, and we did not make such funds available."

blocks.caption: A professional-looking certificate: According to "Glotech GmbH," there was no sponsorship agreement (the graphic, which has since been deleted, was published on Wadim Rosenstein's "X" account in April 2026).Image: X/@WadimRosenstein

blocks.text: Rosenstein is campaigning primarily on the pledge that FIDE would operate "professionally" under his leadership. On his official website, "WR 2026," he promises transparent and direct communication.
DW approached Rosenstein for comment on the financing of his chess activities, but he did not respond.
Political connections
With the support of the DSB and its president, Paul Meyer-Dunker, Rosenstein has succeeded in establishing himself as a serious challenger to the Turlov, the favorite within FIDE.
The 36-year-old also enjoys support from the world of German politics. In early September, Rosenstein met with Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann.
"Joachim Herrmann supports the candidacy of the German applicant Wadim Rosenstein," a subsequently issued statement read.

The Bavarian Interior Ministry told DW that this support related to the "sport-specific focus" of the bid but did not constitute "an assessment of Mr. Rosenstein's private or business activities, nor a prejudgment of any potential reviews by competent authorities."
Online debate cut short

The DSB only learned of the meeting between its FIDE candidate and the Bavarian interior minister after the fact. According to Meyer-Dunker, the DSB supports Rosenstein because he stands for "consistent professionalization" and "greater transparency" within the World Chess Federation. The DSB "has no information regarding Wadim Rosenstein's business activities beyond what has appeared in public reports," Meyer-Dunker said.

Rosenstein had an opportunity to address questions and explain his plans for FIDE's finances in early September. A US chess website had organized an online debate for the candidates. Rosenstein delivered the opening statement; he spoke for just under four minutes, then suddenly exclaimed: "See you in Samarkand!" before cutting the connection.
DW has approached Rosenstein several times to ask why he did not participate in the rest of the discussion regarding FIDE's future. There has been no response to this either.
Dasha Thyssen contributed to this article as a co-author. This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Ethiopia's military says it killed hundreds of TPLF rebels
articles.summary: The TPLF fought against against the Ethiopian military from 2020 to 2022 in a conflict that saw hundreds of thousands of civilians killed. A resumption of fighting has sparked fears of another brutal…

image.caption: Wrecked materiel litters the Tigray Region from several previous wars [FILE: June 20, 2021]Image: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Fighting between Ethiopian troops and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) escalated on Thursday, threatening to shatter a fragile 2022 peace deal.
The renewed fighting first broke out in the Tigray Region in northern Ethiopia on Wednesday.
"We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice president Amanuel Assefa told AFP news agency.
On Thursday, Ethiopia's military said it "launched a counter-offensive that inflicted heavy personnel and equipment losses on the TPLF."

The military said it killed 272 people among the Tigrayan rebels and wounded some 260 more. These figures could not be independently verified, and there was no breakdown given for soldiers and civilians.
Calls for deescelation
The African Union, the United Nations and other international observers have called for restraint and deescelation.

"I am disappointed to see the leadership of the TPLF, that the United States sanctioned earlier this year, make the poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive today," said Ervin J. Massinga, the US ambassador in Addis Ababa.
"Rejecting dialogue sponsored by the African Union under President Obasanjo and engaging in an unwinnable fight does nothing for the people," he added.

blocks.caption: TPLF troops patrolled the regional capital Mekele on WednesdayImage: AFP

blocks.text: What led to the resumption in fighting?
The TPLF was Ethiopia's dominant political force from 1991 until 2018.
It governed with a coalition of other ethnic-based parties, but critics accused it of creating these parties as loyal opposition to sideline preexisting ethnic movements.
When Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office in 2018, he sidelined the TPFL in favor of a government not based on ethnic lines, dominated by his Prosperity Party.
Abiy's early foreign policy saw him repair relations with Ethiopia's former archrival Eritrea — efforts for which he was awarded the Noble Peace Prize in 2019.
But his later determination for landlocked Ethiopia to have access to a seaport was seen as provocative in Eritrea as well in Somalia.
Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again
The TPLF then launched a rebellion against Abiy in 2020, spiraling into a two-year war that saw some 500,000 killed due to violence, famine and the collapse of health services.
During that war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF.

Speaking at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie Amde decried "the forces of destruction and mayhem" and "interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements."

blocks.caption: Ethiopia's President Taye Atske Selassie Amde condemned the brewing conflict at the UN General AssemblyImage: Seth Wenig/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Conflict spreads to Amhara region
Fighting was also reported in the Amhara region in the Ethiopian highlands.
The AFP news agency received reports of fighting around the holy city of Lalibela, home to Ethiopia's ancient, UNESCO-listed rock-hewn churches.
Flights to the popular tourist destination were suspended on Thursday.
Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends?
The TPLF announced an alliance with Amhara's Fano militia, a former foe that has been waging its own insurgency in the region since 2023.

The Fano militia originally emerged as an opponent of TPFL rule and the two sides still have competing claims over land that was absorbed in to the Amhara region from the Tigray region after the last war.
"The only issue joining them is their opposition to Prosperity Party rule," said Kjetil Tronvoll, a professor of peace and conflict studies at Oslo New ⁠University College.

articles.title: Trump swoons over strongman soulmate Xi – are you feeling jealous, Vladimir?
articles.summary:
Deference was deafening as US president rolled out red carpet for world’s biggest jailer of journalists – perhaps he was seeking tips

One is an authoritarian who represses the media with a…

blocks.text: One is an authoritarian who represses the media with a strong allergy to democratic elections. The other is head of the Chinese Communist party.

Donald Trump welcomed the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to the White House on Thursday, setting the stage for a scene quite unlike anything the august old building has seen over more than two centuries.
“Remarkably,” observed the US president, “this is our first time meeting together here at the White House, and as President Xi has already seen, a lot has changed since he was last here.”

While Xi remained poker-faced, only a brief look around a grand foyer bedecked with American and Chinese flags would have verified Trump’s statement. On one wall, where an official portrait of Barack Obama once hung, was the dramatic image of a bloodied Trump with fist raised urging his supporters to “fight!” after a failed assassination attempt.

And while Chinese state media had been welcomed onto the White House grounds, many US journalists had not, thanks to Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico. Michael McFaul, a former US diplomat, described the vivid contrast as “wrong and embarrassing”.

That was hard to deny, given that China ranks 178th in Reporters Without Borders’ press freedom index, ahead of only North Korea and Eritrea (the US, for the record, is down to 64th). But it also made perfect sense because, whereas past presidents sought to make China more like the US, Trump evidently aspires to make the US more like China.

blocks.caption: Trump and Xi walk along the Colonnade at the White House. Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/Abaca/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The deference was deafening. On Wednesday night he and his wife, Melania, travelled to Joint Base Andrews in Maryland to greet Xi off his plane – a schlep that US presidents rarely make for foreign leaders – and rolled out a literal red carpet for his strongman soulmate.
Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, observed on X: “If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll roll out the red carpet for you…”
Vladimir, are you feeling jealous yet?

“I met President Xi at the plane (Airport!) yesterday and he looks strong, vibrant, and fit — Better than ever,” a gooey-eyed Trump gushed on his Truth Social patform. “Madam Xi, of course, BEAUTIFUL!”
Protocol error! Protocol error! When the president wrote “Madam Xi”, referring to Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, he should have said “Madame Peng”, which is how she is recognised.

Xi is such a star that he got two welcomes. On Thursday morning, there were more flags, more trumpet blasts, and another red carpet as the Trumps emerged from the White House south portico to greet Xi and Peng.

Then it was on to the grand foyer for statements – with no reporter questions allowed, of course – before the two delegations, including Vice-President JD Vance and wife Usha, sitting in neat rows. Trump went first. You can tell when he’s on his best behaviour because he (mostly) sticks to the teleprompter. The interpreter must have been relieved that he did not have to match Trump, weave for weave.

blocks.caption: The presidents meet with their delegations at the Oval Office. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP

blocks.text: Trump touted his “truly ⁠great friendship” with Xi and claimed the two countries ⁠had made strides on trade since his trip ​to China in May. “During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and ‘super intelligence,’” he said, using his alternative name for artificial intelligence. If Xi felt like rolling his eyes at that, he managed to resist.

The president, ever nostalgic for the 20th century, suggested that the second world war offers a lesson on how the competitors can work together. “Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country,” he said, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that helped defend China against Japanese invasion. “They were just unbelievable.”
He added that it was US marines’ interactions with Chinese citizens that inspired them “to adopt a Chinese phrase that they still use today: gung ho”.
Rarely does Trump appear at an event and not end up behind the microphone for longer than any other speaker on the bill.

But it was Xi, speaking more substantially, who looked like he owned the place. Trump, sitting behind with hands clasped together, had the appearance of junior partner. Xi said he was ready to work with the president to “steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course toward the future”.
Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!
Xi had a charm offensive of his own. “President Trump and I have respect for each other,” he said. “We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”

He announced Thursday that 100,000 young American students would be invited to study in China over the next five years. Better still, he revealed China will sent two giant pandas – Ping Ping and Fuchuan – to a zoo in Atlanta.

Then he got to the meat in the sandwich, insisting that the countries can “co-exist in peace” and their competition “should be a healthy one”. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome,” Xi declared, in a tacit acknowledgement that China is threatening to displace the US as the world’s superpower.

blocks.caption: Trump speaks to reporters after walking with Xi to show him Marine One at the White House. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: But with more flattery, he added: “Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand.”

Next up was a military ceremony including a flyover at the Rose Garden, with Chinese flags waving from the Oval Office roof alongside US flags. A marching band dressed in the garb of the Revolutionary War era – tricorn hats, white wigs, red tunics – paraded in the paved over Rose Garden (another change since Xi’s last visit).

None of this was covered by the usual cable news networks because they were boycotting shared coverage, in solidarity with the banned outlets. If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound? If a democracy falls and no one is around to film it, does it make a yelp?
Trump then sat down with the world’s biggest jailer of journalists for bilateral talks. Perhaps he was seeking tips.
When they met face to face, was this a Reagan-Gorbachev style summit of great historical import, discussing guardrails on AI and other ways not to destroy the world? Maybe not.

Showing off the Marine One helicopter and his new helipad on the south lawn, Trump reported: “We had a great meeting - and he has a great interest in granite. He likes granite. He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite.”
Not even Xi had been spared the dreaded tour of Trump’s architectural follies.

By the afternoon, some of the banned reporters had been allowed back on to the White House campus after a judge found Trump’s action to be unconstitutional. It must have been a tricky one to explain to Xi. He remains the master of repression; Trump is merely The Apprentice.

articles.title: Watch: UN delegates walk out of Netanyahu speech
articles.summary: The Israeli delegation could be be seen cheering in support during Netanyahu's speech.

blocks.text: Dozens of United Nations delegates walked out of the hall Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was due to deliver a speech in.
Addressing the UN's General Assembly in New York, Netanyahu described those walking out as "moral cowards". Those who remained and felt similarly should leave, he said.
The Israeli delegation could be seen cheering Netanyahu in support.

Israel has faced condemnation for its actions in Gaza and Lebanon. A UN commission of inquiry has previously accused Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza - Israel has strongly rejected the accusations.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,920 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry.

articles.title: Why Australia chose the world's biggest political stage to reveal OpenAI hack
articles.summary: Australia, which has strict social media restrictions and has proposed controls on algorithms and smart glasses, announced the breach at the UN.

blocks.text: It's entirely possible other governments have been the victim of rogue AI agents.
Former Australian government cybersecurity adviser Alastair MacGibbon told the BBC he'd heard whispers that several others have been notified of similar recent breaches by OpenAI agents.

"Some have chosen to not be public – that's every government's choice on how it wants to handle these things," the CyberCX chief strategy officer said. "The [Australian] government chose a time to release this to gain maximum publicity which is their wont to do."

Revealing a data breach can of course be a risky strategy for governments - it leaves them vulnerable to criticism that their security systems aren't up to scratch. But the fact that no sensitive information was leaked put Australia in a stronger position to use the incident.

"Nobody has died," says the University of Queensland's associate professor Michael Noetel, who studies AI risks. "This is another canary in the coal mine. This sort of loss-of-control incident, even though it's minor now, is what CEOs are worried about getting worse over time."

Though Australia has made a name for itself by taking a stand against social media companies, taking up the AI mantle now is another way for Australia to rein in big tech, says Tama Leaver, professor of internet studies at Curtin University in Perth.
"It's impossible to say for sure, but it seems incredibly likely that this was very carefully planned."

articles.title: Would you wear an air-quality sensor on your body?
articles.summary: In this issue of our environmental newsletter, we check out some wearable art that makes air pollution highly visible; map out where and when this year's El Nino is expected to be a killer; and learn…

image.caption: Grace Grothaus, postdoctoral researcher at York University, puts on her AtmoSpheres 01 prototype. (Anand Ram/CBC News)

blocks.text: Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.
Hi, it's Anand. I think about air quality a lot since the pandemic and our seemingly yearly bouts with wildfire smoke. But how do you get more people thinking about dangers you can't always see?
This week:

items: Would you wear an air-quality warning on your body?
The Big Picture: Killer El Niño
Solar power on an Arctic scrapyard

blocks.text: Would you wear an air-quality warning on your body?
If it weren't for the pillowy white blobs and clear tubing, I'd say Grace Grothaus was putting on a kind of lead apron.
But as it lights up, bright green in the shape of a pair of lungs, it tells me my real lungs, here in her small office in Toronto, are safe from invisible but harmful air pollutants.

"The illumination of the lungs sort of brings the atmosphere that we can't see into the body and makes it something that is suddenly visible," explains Grothaus, an artist and scientist with York University.

This prototype, Grothaus says, was developed while she was doing her master's degree at the University of California San Diego. It uses a small sensor at the back to draw in air and check for two forms of pollution, PM2.5 and black carbon (microscopic soot, essentially). Both can be hazardous to human health.
The sensor information is then translated to the front lighting, following the colour scheme of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's air quality index (AQI).
"So you have green, the level where the air is safe to breathe," Grothaus said.
It then progresses through yellow, orange, red, purple and brown.
"We rarely see those later-stage colours, such as red and purple, except during wildfire season."

But wildfire smoke — even for Canadians who now find themselves having to deal with it almost every year — isn't the only kind of danger in the air. Experts have said for years that there's no safe level of any particulate matter, and the risk is present even as a result of such things as traffic congestion.
But the challenge is that the pollutants are often invisible — a gap that some artists are trying to fill.
"All of them get forgotten," said Michael Pinsky, a visual artist based in London. Pinsky has been using the environment and climate change as messages in his installations for two decades.

His work ranges from dredging bikes and shopping carts out of a Parisian canal to his latest, Your Shit Smells Like Roses, a project highlighting how black water (toilet waste) can be beneficial when it's separated from the grey water that contains the soaps and detergents we also flush down the drain.

His Pollution Pods tackled pollution through a series of connected geodesic domes recreating the air of different cities. He worked with a fragrance company to recreate smells such as sulphur, but also adjusted the temperature and humidity to mimic the experience he wanted: the shock of getting off a plane into a different city.

"In many ways, we have habituated to pollution," Pinsky said, recalling how some people had their senses shocked after going through it. "It's that lack of being able to habituate to it that makes it a kind of powerful, visceral experience."
And art can be a change-maker.

"There's scientific reasoning showing why climate change is happening, but the reason why it's happening is cultural," Pinsky told me via video call from London, suggesting the climate message needs a different tactic.
"You have to move beyond, ‘Oh wow, the whole world's going to blow up.' You have to make it unfashionable to do certain things."
Back in Toronto, Grothaus is now working on a portable air quality sensor called AirWear, which serves as a more of a community-focused everyday device.

Part of its development involved design workshops with people living between Toronto's downtown Billy Bishop airport and its busy Gardiner Expressway. Participants said that they wanted something light and with a positive message, leading Grothaus to redesign the AirWear as a friendlier-looking cloud shape.
She hopes to recruit some more participants from the community for a two-week real-world pilot of these devices before the year's end.
"Art can make things felt or seen," Grothaus said. "But community research can make it useful."
— Anand Ram
Old issues of What on Earth? are here. The CBC News climate page is here.

Check out our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode: As Parliament gets back in session, there's a lot going on: a trade war, talk of Alberta separation and international alliances being redrawn. Prime Minister Mark Carney has been clear: he doesn't think the old climate plan he inherited from the Trudeau government holds up to Canada's new reality.

So, where does climate fit in what Carney calls the next "world order?" Two of our political journalists, David Thurton and Aaron Wherry, break down what we know so far and what they're watching for next.
LISTEN | There's a lot on Carney's plate. Is our climate plan cooked?:

Reader feedback
Got questions, comments, or just want to share something? Write us at whatonearth@cbc.ca (and send photos there, too!)
The Big Picture: Killer El Niño

We've been warned of a "super" El Niño for months. Now, after smashing its previous temperature record months before its expected peak, we're getting a forecast of the potential human toll. Researchers at the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago say that between June 2026 and February 2027, the world will see 451,000 more deaths than expected from heat-related causes, because of El Niño. The map above shows how many more deaths are expected in countries compared to the last two decades.

The worst impacts will be felt in the global South, such as Nigeria and Indonesia. The experts say the time to act is now, using "heat warnings, health outreach to vulnerable populations, cooling centres and hydration stations, worker protections, and expanded health system capacity" to help people cope with extreme heat.
Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

items: Outgoing UN Secretary General António Guterres may have a couple more months left in his tenure, but he is at his final General Assembly, and besides delivering a searing address that called out the U.S., sat down for a much more frank exit interview with the Guardian — proving his outspoken critique of fossil fuel companies has not wavered in the face of international climate rollbacks.

After a hurricane, multi-million dollar mansions are replacing homes destroyed in the disaster. Inside Climate News looks at why "post-disaster gentrification" happens and what it means for communities hit by floods or wildfires.
A fascinating new citizen reporting project called Who Eats Whom wants your pictures of animals eating lunch. Try looking up your preferred species — just don't do it at mealtimes!

The Pembina Institute's Tim Weis and his family took a 2,800-kilometre EV roadtrip from Edmonton to Ucluelet, B.C., this summer in a Volkswagen ID.4. He shares his experience, including what planning and charging was like, how it compares to how it used to be, and what could still use improvement.

blocks.text: Ikayuut solar and energy storage project now complete in Naujaat
In a reclaimed scrapyard in Naujaat, Nunavut, the Ikayuut solar and energy storage project has flipped the switch to renewable energy.
The project is the first to reach operation from Qulliq Energy Corporation's (QEC) independent power producer program (IPP), which allows communities to sell renewable energy to QEC's power grid.
Now that the project is operational, QEC CEO Ernest Douglas said it will help the community reduce its diesel consumption by 30 per cent or 400,000 litres per year.
In a statement, Sakku Investments Corporation said the project is a powerful example of turning a challenge into an opportunity.
"A piece of land that was previously contaminated and not readily usable has been transformed into something productive that can provide value to the community," the statement said.
"Our goal is not simply to introduce new energy technologies into our communities but to build Inuit capacity and create opportunities for Kivalliqmiut to have a greater role in the energy sector."

The project started supplying energy to Naujaat's power grid on Aug. 20 and is a collaboration between Kivalliq Alternative Energy, Sakku Investments Corporation, Northern Energy Capital, QEC and the hamlet of Naujaat.
"It's just a testament of what can happen when QEC works with communities, renewable energy developers and Inuit organizations so that we can reduce our diesel consumption," Douglas said.

James Griffiths, the director of development at Northern Energy Capital, said what's unique about this project is that on a bright sunny day when the battery storage is charged, there is the possibility to turn off the diesel generators.
"At that point in time, they could shut the diesel generator off and rely on the sun that's shining," Griffiths said. "This would be a momentous first moment, when QEC first turns its diesel off."
Douglas said turning off the diesel generators could potentially happen next summer.

"[We still] need for the diesel generators to provide the backbone that they will always serve in our communities for reliable electricity. But the goal here is to continue to reduce our reliance on imported diesel fuel," Douglas said.
Solar panels built for the cold
Construction took two years to complete, and Griffiths said though the project is new, the technology itself is tried and tested.
"Solar panels are operating in all kinds of climates today and they're very reliable," he said.
"Solar panels actually operate more efficiently when they're cold. There are some technologies that deliberately cool solar panels for that reason."
In the winter, Griffiths said the project is winterized so that the solar panels can withstand the cold climate.
Both Douglas and Griffiths said there are many opportunities for renewable energy projects in Nunavut in the future, including with the IPP program.

"Ultimately, the vision is to consume local energy at the place where it's derived," Douglas said. "We still need to have the diesel generation as a backup, but the potential to unlock renewable energy to continue to reduce that diesel consumption — it's exciting in Nunavut."
— Bianca McKeown
